# Self-Evolving Coding Agents

Hao Zhou¹   Haichuan Hu¹   Tianyu Luo²   Ye Shang²  
Chunrong Fang²   Zhenyu Chen²   Liang Xiao¹   Quanjun Zhang¹

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have moved software automation beyond code
generation toward coding agents that inspect repositories, invoke tools,
run tests, and repair failures. Yet many agents remain episodic, using
feedback to solve the current task without changing how they approach
the next one. Software engineering offers a particularly suitable
setting for overcoming this limitation. Execution provides concrete
outcomes and diagnostics, while coding trajectories and versioned
repositories make experience traceable and often reproducible.
Self-evolving coding agents use such experience to update the reusable
components that shape their later work. This survey distinguishes these
agent updates from changes to task code and identifies assets,
architecture, and model parameters as progressively deeper intervention
targets. As intervention deepens, a lesson can influence more decisions
and become harder to attribute or reverse. We examine coding signals and
adoption timing alongside this taxonomy to show how similar feedback can
produce different updates and when those changes begin to shape later
execution. Early adoption can use fresh feedback but may rely on
incomplete evidence, while waiting permits broader validation but delays
reuse. Finally, we examine benchmarks and emerging products, finding
that practical systems favor inspectable assets and editable harnesses
while evaluation still centers largely on individual task outcomes.
Passing tests support the current software artifact under checked
conditions; showing that an agent has improved requires evidence that
retained changes benefit later decisions.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models have moved software automation beyond code
generation ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib57), [Austin et al.,
2021](#bib.bib58)) toward agents that inspect repositories, use
command-line tools, revise files, and test candidate patches. SWE-agent,
OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, and related repair systems exemplify this
shift toward repository-level execution ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib7),
[Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib8), [Zhang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib10),
[Bouzenia et al., 2024](#bib.bib11), [Arora et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)).
Benchmarks based on real issues make the resulting repairs measurable,
while tying each outcome to a particular repository and environment
([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib6), [Deng et al., 2025](#bib.bib17),
[Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib170)). Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents") places this
development alongside the broader rise of self-evolving agents. The
unresolved step is what happens beyond the immediate repair. An agent
may use a failed test to fix one patch yet carry no reusable change into
later tasks, a limitation that motivates experience-driven issue
resolution ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20)). Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
sketches the feedback and update loop at issue.

![Refer to caption](2608.03392v4/self-evolving-code-agent.png)

Figure 2: Overview of self-evolving coding agents.

Coding offers unusually concrete evidence for studying this step. Tests
provide executable outcomes; compiler messages and stack traces narrow
failures; and trajectories record the searches, edits, and retries that
preceded a patch ([Pan et al., 2025](#bib.bib51), [Jain et al.,
2025](#bib.bib53), [Garg and Huang, 2026](#bib.bib16), [Bouzenia and
Pradel, 2024](#bib.bib15)). Issues, diffs, and versioned repositories
connect those observations to the software conditions under which they
arose ([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)). Recorded dependencies and
tool versions can make many observations re-executable, although
changing environments limit that reproducibility ([Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24), [Eliseeva et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)). Specific,
traceable feedback is still incomplete feedback. A passing test checks
only selected behavior, and functional success need not establish patch
quality or security ([Chen and Jiang, 2024](#bib.bib192), [Wei et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib23)). Interpreting this evidence requires distinguishing
changes to the program being built from changes to the agent that builds
it. The first change is visible in a patch and its validation results.
The second requires an experience-derived update to a reusable agent
component, followed by its use in later execution. Earlier agent
research showed how reflection and stored experience can inform later
attempts ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib33), [Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26), [Wang et al., 2025e](#bib.bib166)); coding-specific
systems now retain repair knowledge across issues ([Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib20)). We use _self-evolving coding agent_ for a system
whose retained updates improve subsequent coding behavior. A successful
patch may yield an overgeneralized memory, while an unsuccessful attempt
may contain a useful diagnosis. The current artifact’s result therefore
cannot by itself establish the value of an agent update.

The same debugging experience can enter an agent at different depths.
SWE-Exp and Repository Memory retain information for later retrieval,
while CODESKILL and Socratic-SWE turn trajectories into reusable
procedures ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20), [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib21), [Li et al., 2026c](#bib.bib43), [Xiao et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib45)). Live-SWE-agent creates callable utilities during
issue resolution ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). Other methods revise
the execution structure, as in source-level agent evolution, workflow
search, harness repair, or team coordination ([Zhang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib18), [Zhang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib40), [Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib75), [Hu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib38)); Agent-RLVR and
SWE-RL instead update model parameters using coding feedback ([Da et
al., 2025](#bib.bib52), [Wei et al., 2026b](#bib.bib55)). We organize
these targets as assets, architecture, and model parameters. The
ordering reflects typical intervention depth: a resource can often be
edited locally, whereas changes to control flow or learned policy can
affect more decisions. Depth does not guarantee benefit. The update
target alone does not explain how evolution occurs. Coding signals
determine what evidence a method consumes, while adoption timing
determines how much evidence is available before a change enters
execution. A utility can be created within a task, team instructions can
change between development rounds, experience can be retained after an
issue, and a model update can aggregate trajectories across tasks ([Xia
et al., 2025](#bib.bib19), [Hu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib38), [Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib20), [Da et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)). Earlier adoption
allows a rapid response to local feedback; later adoption permits
broader validation but delays reuse.

Evaluation must determine whether a retained change helped after reuse,
rather than crediting it for the task that produced it. Issue-resolution
benchmarks measure patches, while sequential agent benchmarks make
persistence and later-task behavior part of the protocol ([Jimenez et
al., 2023](#bib.bib6), [Deng et al., 2025](#bib.bib17), [Jiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib176), [Xue et al., 2026](#bib.bib175), [Zhang et al.,
2026m](#bib.bib174)). Coding tasks and their tests may also be used to
construct updates, select candidates, and report final performance.
Reusing related cases across these roles can make adaptation to an
evaluator look like general progress. Studies of harness evolution
further show why search budgets and harness choice matter when
attributing a gain ([Wang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib184), [Vats and Golev,
2026](#bib.bib186), [Ben Sghaier et al., 2026](#bib.bib185)). An
evolution study should therefore identify what persists, compare updated
and frozen agents under matched conditions on held-out tasks, and report
regressions and costs alongside gains. Those controls separate
improvement from extra attempts, computation, or familiarity with
evaluation cases.

#### Relation to Existing Surveys

Existing surveys examine either agents that evolve across domains or
agents that perform software-engineering tasks. General
self-evolving-agent surveys discuss programming alongside many other
applications, without centering the distinctive evidence produced by
tests, diagnostics, and versioned repositories ([Gao et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib28), [Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)).
Software-engineering agent surveys instead organize development tasks,
architectures, and collaboration; retaining an experience-derived agent
update is not their inclusion criterion ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib30),
[Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib31)). This distinction matters because
coding work can change both the project under repair and the agent that
repairs it. _Code as Agent Harness_ recognizes code as agent
infrastructure, but studies that substrate across multiple domains
([Ning and others, 2026](#bib.bib32)). Our unit of analysis is the
persistent change to a coding agent produced by software-engineering
experience. We ask which component retains it, what software evidence
motivates it, when it is adopted, and whether its reuse improves later
coding behavior. A correct patch establishes a result for one task; it
does not establish that the agent learned a useful capability. Table
[1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Relation to Existing Surveys ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
compares these boundaries.

| Survey                                                                    | Main focus                                | Persistent agent update      | Role of coding                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| _General self-evolving agents_ ([Gao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib28))          | Evolution mechanisms across domains       | Central                      | One application domain           |
| _Comprehensive self-evolving AI agents_ ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)) | Feedback-driven agent-system optimization | Central                      | One specialized domain           |
| _LLM agents for SE_ ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib30))                      | LLM agent designs and SE tasks            | Not required                 | Core task setting                |
| _Agents in SE_ ([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib31))                         | Agent applications and roles in SE        | Not required                 | Core task setting                |
| _Code as Agent Harness_ ([Ning and others, 2026](#bib.bib32))             | Code-based agent infrastructure           | One mechanism                | Cross-domain execution substrate |
| Our Survey                                                                | Coding-agent updates and later benefit    | Required; tested after reuse | Update and evaluation evidence   |

Table 1: Comparison of related surveys by focus, persistent updates, and
the role of coding.

This survey makes three contributions that connect the target of
evolution, the coding evidence behind an update, and the evaluation of
its later effects:

- •
  Definition and target taxonomy. We distinguish changes to the coding
  agent from changes to the code it produces. We then classify
  persistent agent updates as changes to assets, architecture, or model
  parameters, ordered by intervention depth.
- •
  Coding signals and update mechanisms. We classify the evidence
  available during software development and examine how methods turn it
  into persistent updates. We also compare when updates are adopted,
  showing how timing affects the evidence available before reuse.
- •
  Evaluation of agent improvement. We distinguish success on the current
  coding task from improvement caused by a retained update. Our analysis
  of benchmarks identifies the matched, held-out, and longitudinal
  comparisons needed to measure later gains, regressions, and costs.

The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section
[2](#S2 "2 Background and Definitions ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
defines coding agents and self-evolving agents, then specifies the
retention, reuse, and improvement requirements that distinguish
self-evolving coding agents. Section
[3](#S3 "3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
introduces the target-centered taxonomy and explains the different
depths of asset, architecture, and model updates, then profiles the
surveyed methods by year and publication outlet. Section
[4](#S4 "4 Assets Self-Evolution ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents") reviews
how memory, skills, tools, and context evolve. Section
[5](#S5 "5 Architecture Self-Evolution ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
examines changes to harnesses, workflows, and multi-agent coordination,
while Section
[6](#S6 "6 Model Self-Evolution ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
addresses parameter adaptation. Section
[7](#S7 "7 Coding Feedback and Evolution Dynamics ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
analyzes coding signals, how methods turn them into persistent changes,
and when those changes are adopted. Section
[8](#S8 "8 Benchmarks and Evaluation ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
reviews benchmarks and the controls needed to measure later benefit.
Section
[9](#S9 "9 Self-Evolving Coding Products ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
examines how products expose and govern updates. Section
[10](#S10 "10 Challenges and Open Problems ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
discusses open problems in feedback validity, reversibility, and
generalization, and Section
[11](#S11 "11 Conclusion ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents") concludes.

## 2 Background and Definitions

Coding agents perform software development tasks by interacting with
repositories, tools, and execution environments, while the agents
themselves are built from code, configurations, and model parameters.
Code thus plays a dual role: it is both a product of task solving and
part of the system that solves the task. This dual role allows coding
capabilities to act on both task artifacts and the agent itself, but
modifying code does not inherently constitute self-evolution. The key
distinction is whether a change extends beyond improving the current
solution to persistently changing how subsequent tasks are solved.
Self-evolving agents embody this experience- and feedback-driven
adaptation of the agent itself. Self-evolving coding agents ground that
process in coding practice: task solving generates experience,
experience drives agent updates, and retained updates guide subsequent
coding activity. The object of evolution is the agent, not merely the
programs it generates or modifies.

### 2.1 Coding Agents

A coding agent is an LLM-based system that pursues software development
objectives through actions in a development environment. It decides what
information to obtain, what changes to make, and how to assess their
effects. Repository-level tasks require reasoning across existing files
and dependencies ([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)), often with context
gathered during task execution. SWE-agent and OpenHands support this
process through interfaces for repository navigation, editing, and
execution ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib7), [Wang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib8)). Interaction serves both to modify software and to
investigate its behavior: even an unsuccessful repair can provide
evidence that guides the next attempt.

The surrounding system shapes what the model can observe and do, and how
its decisions are organized. CodeAct expresses actions through
executable code ([Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib14)), AutoCodeRover
retrieves context through structured code search ([Zhang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib10)), and Debug2Fix exposes runtime behavior through
interactive debugging ([Garg and Huang, 2026](#bib.bib16)). MetaGPT
coordinates specialized development roles ([Hong et al.,
2023](#bib.bib9)), while MASAI assigns distinct objectives and
strategies to modules ([Arora et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)). SGAgent
bridges fault localization and patch generation with explicit,
context-informed repair suggestions ([Zhang et al.,
2026f](#bib.bib123)); Trae Agent organizes candidate generation,
pruning, and selection ([Trae Research Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib162)).
The value of these arrangements lies in the decisions they enable,
alongside their computational cost. Agentless offers a useful
comparison: a fixed localization, repair, and validation pipeline can
also achieve competitive repair results ([Xia et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13)).

### 2.2 Self-Evolving Agents

A self-evolving agent uses experience and feedback to update its own
reusable state or components, allowing past interactions to shape
subsequent behavior. Updates can affect memory, skills, tools,
architecture, or model parameters ([Fang et al., 2025](#bib.bib29), [Gao
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib28)). Experience both informs current actions and
provides a basis for revising how the agent will act again. These
revisions persist as part of its memory, capabilities, or decision
process beyond the interaction that produced them.

Experience can support adaptation without changing model weights: ExpeL
extracts reusable insights ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)), Voyager
accumulates composable executable skills ([Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib35)), and Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable routines
from task trajectories ([Wang et al., 2025e](#bib.bib166)). A-MEM
further revises existing memories and their links as new experiences
arrive ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib167)). Adaptation also reaches control
logic through Gödel Agent’s modification of its own implementation ([Yin
et al., 2025](#bib.bib163)). Policy learning offers another route: WebRL
builds an online training curriculum from unsuccessful web interactions
([Qi et al., 2025](#bib.bib164)), while Tool-R0 co-evolves a task
generator and a tool-using solver through self-play reinforcement
learning ([Acikgoz et al., 2026](#bib.bib165)). These mechanisms turn
experience into changes that subsequent execution can use. A retained
record contributes to self-evolution when it participates in this
update-and-reuse process; storage alone is insufficient. Reuse may occur
within a continuing task or across tasks, and human feedback or approval
can accompany system-generated updates. Retention and reuse establish an
adaptation mechanism, while reliable gains require evidence from
evaluating the updated agent.

### 2.3 Self-Evolving Coding Agents

Coding agents acquire experience as they inspect repositories, execute
programs, and revise solutions. This experience can help complete the
current task, but it can also inform changes to the system performing
the task. Self-evolving coding agents connect software task execution
with improvement of the agent itself, turning coding experience into
retained updates whose reuse improves subsequent coding performance.
Task solving supplies both software artifacts and experience from which
the agent can develop further capabilities.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To distinguish changes to the task solution from changes to the agent,
we represent the reusable agent configuration at adaptation round $`t`$
as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathcal{A}_{t}=(\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t},\theta_{t}),
       ```                                                            |     | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$ denotes assets (memory, skills, tools, and
context), $`\mathcal{H}_{t}`$ denotes architecture (harness, workflow,
and multi-agent organization), and $`\theta_{t}`$ denotes model
parameters. These components correspond to the three categories of
evolution targets in our taxonomy and jointly shape the agent’s
capabilities and decision process. For a software task $`q`$ in
environment $`\mathcal{E}`$, execution is represented by

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(z_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t})=\operatorname{Execute}(\mathcal{A}_{t},q,\mathcal{E}).
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`z_{t}`$ is the software artifact produced or revised,
$`\tau_{t}`$ records the agent’s actions and resulting observations, and
$`f_{t}`$ denotes feedback on execution and its outcomes. The artifact
is the immediate result of task solving; the trajectory and feedback
also provide experience for revising the system that produced it.

An update mechanism $`\mathcal{U}`$ uses this experience to propose
changes to the reusable agent configuration:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{t+1}=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{A}_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}).
``` |  | (3) |

The candidate may revise one or several components of
$`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$ while leaving the others unchanged. The tilde
distinguishes a proposed configuration from one adopted for subsequent
execution. A proposal may be accepted, revised, or discarded; for a
single candidate, adoption is expressed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{A}_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{t+1},&\text{if the candidate is accepted},\\
\mathcal{A}_{t},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (4) |

Acceptance retains the candidate’s changes in $`\mathcal{A}_{t+1}`$,
making them available to guide later execution. Rejection preserves the
existing configuration, while revision produces another candidate for
consideration.

A single coding task can involve several rounds of adaptation, and the
effects of one update may extend to multiple later tasks; $`t`$
therefore indexes adaptation rounds. An agent may use experience gained
during an ongoing task to adjust its remaining work ([Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)), or retain those adjustments for future tasks.
Persistence allows experience to have an effect beyond the operation
that produced the update, giving a coding attempt the potential to
change how the agent solves problems later. Yet retained changes may
encode useful strategies or mistaken generalizations from local
experience. Only when their subsequent use improves problem-solving
capability, reliability, or efficiency can the agent be said to have
progressed through experience, rather than merely accumulated changes.

#### The operational boundary

We identify self-evolving coding agents using four criteria that examine
how code-related experience changes the agent itself and whether reusing
those changes improves subsequent coding performance:

1.  (1)
    Update target. The change must affect an identifiable component of
    $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$. Repairing a failing patch or making a target
    program faster changes the task artifact $`z_{t}`$. Self-Refine’s
    code-refinement loop revises generated outputs ([Madaan et al.,
    2023](#bib.bib34)); AlphaEvolve’s search over candidate algorithms
    likewise optimizes task programs ([Novikov et al.,
    2025](#bib.bib49)). These operations alone constitute task solving.
2.  (2)
    Update source. The system must generate updates from code-related
    experience and feedback, such as repository interactions, execution
    traces, or test results.
3.  (3)
    Update reuse. Updates must be retained as agent components and
    actually used in later coding execution, within the same task or
    across tasks. Storage alone is insufficient.
4.  (4)
    Capability improvement. Reusing the updates must improve the agent’s
    problem-solving capability, reliability, or efficiency in subsequent
    coding activity, supported by comparisons with the pre-update agent
    under comparable conditions.

#### From retained experience to behavioral influence

We analyze improvement through five links: *experience collection,
component update, subsequent use, behavioral change, and effect
evaluation*. These links help locate where an evolution mechanism
succeeds or breaks down. Collection supplies observations, while
updating converts them into reusable components. This transition
requires deciding what to retain and which conditions govern its
applicability. Subsequent use brings the update into execution, but use
alone does not establish contribution. A retrieved memory may repeat
available information, and an invoked skill may recommend an action the
agent would have taken anyway. Let $`\pi_{\mathcal{A}}(\cdot\mid x)`$
denote the agent’s action-selection distribution at a matched decision
state $`x`$. The behavioral difference induced by an update can be
expressed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{t}(x)=d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{t+1}}(\cdot\mid x),\pi_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}(\cdot\mid x)\right),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`d_{\mathrm{TV}}`$ is the total variation distance between
probability distributions. Here, actions may include tool calls, code
edits, or other execution choices. A value of $`\delta_{t}(x)=0`$
indicates unchanged action probabilities at that state, while
$`\delta_{t}(x)>0`$ indicates a behavioral change without establishing
its benefit. To assess improvement, let $`\mathcal{D}`$ denote an
evaluation distribution over tasks or matched continuation states within
the intended scope of reuse, $`B`$ a common execution budget, and
$`s(\mathcal{A},q;B)`$ a performance score on case $`q`$, with higher
values indicating better performance. The expected gain is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta J_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[s(\mathcal{A}_{t+1},q;B)-s(\mathcal{A}_{t},q;B)\right].
``` |  | (6) |

The expectation also averages over execution randomness. Evidence for
$`\Delta J_{t}>0`$ supports an average improvement under the specified
scope and budget. A larger behavioral difference need not yield a larger
gain. Coding introduces a further gap between the scope of feedback and
the scope of reuse. Tests evaluate a concrete software artifact, whereas
an agent update may influence many future decisions. A successful patch
does not by itself validate a reusable debugging rule derived from it.
Effective evolution therefore requires preserving relevant conditions
when abstracting experience and aligning $`\mathcal{D}`$ with the
claimed scope of reuse. The five links expose where useful evidence may
be lost, overgeneralized, or fail to influence subsequent behavior.

#### How coding shapes evolution

Coding interactions connect the agent’s problem-solving decisions with
actual execution outcomes, providing a verifiable basis for experience
formation. Test failures expose limitations of the current solution
while also providing evidence for examining the decisions made during
task solving and their consequences. Analysis of historical repairs
further supports the identification of effective strategies and their
applicable conditions, turning experience from individual tasks into
reusable repair knowledge (e.g., SWE-Exp ([Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib20)), EvoRepair ([Hu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), and
Repository Memory ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21))). Translating
experience into agent updates involves using this knowledge to shape
subsequent learning and execution. Repair patterns can be abstracted
into reusable guidance, while recurring execution problems can inform
the proposal and validation of changes to how the agent operates (e.g.,
CODESKILL ([Li et al., 2026c](#bib.bib43)), Socratic-SWE ([Xiao et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib45)), Self-Harness ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib97)),
and AutoSaddler ([Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib147))). Experience is
context-dependent, and its reuse beyond the original conditions requires
further execution evidence to assess and refine the applicability of the
retained knowledge. Table
[2](#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ How coding shapes evolution ‣ 2.3 Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ 2 Background and Definitions ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
summarizes the defining requirements of the three agent concepts.

| Agent Type | Coding Tasks | Agent Updates | Updates from Coding | Retention and Reuse |  Verified Coding Gains |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Coding Agents | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |  ✗ |
| Self-Evolving Agents | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |  ✗ |
| Self-Evolving Coding Agents | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |  ✓ |

Table 2: Defining requirements across the three agent concepts.

## 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents

Coding experience can improve an agent by changing the resources it can
use, the organization of its execution, or the parameters underlying its
decisions. Following
$`\mathcal{A}_{t}=(\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t},\theta_{t})`$, we
organize these targets into Assets Self-Evolution, Architecture
Self-Evolution, and Model Self-Evolution. Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
presents the three categories, their subcategories, and representative
works. Assets evolution changes *what is available*, for example by
adding a tool, revising a skill, or refining memory and context.
Architecture evolution changes *how execution is organized*, including
the harness, workflow, and collaboration among agents. Model evolution
changes *the parameterized policy* that shapes decisions within this
system. This ordering reflects progressively deeper intervention in the
agent’s implementation. Assets are typically modular resources that can
be added, revised, or replaced within an existing execution structure.
Architecture updates reach into the code or configuration governing
execution, changing control flow, stage dependencies, or coordination
among agents. Model updates reach further into the learned parameters
underlying action selection. The progression thus moves from modifying
available resources, through restructuring the system that uses them, to
updating its learned decision mechanism. Tool updates may also involve
code, but they revise available operations, while architecture updates
change how the system organizes and controls execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Hierarchical taxonomy of self-evolving coding agents by the
primary persistent target of evolution: Assets Self-Evolution (blue),
Architecture Self-Evolution (orange), and Model Self-Evolution (purple).
The leaf nodes cover all 108 papers in Section 1 of the companion
repository’s taxonomy, using abbreviated titles and citations to
identify each work.

### 3.1 Assets Self-Evolution

Assets comprise the reusable information and capabilities that support
coding activity. We represent the asset state as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{S}_{t}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{t},\mathcal{K}_{t},\mathcal{T}_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t}\right),\qquad\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}_{t+1}=\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{S}}(\mathcal{A}_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}),
``` |  | (7) |

where $`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$, $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$, $`\mathcal{T}_{t}`$, and
$`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$ denote memory, skills, tools, and context,
respectively. Memory retains knowledge acquired from prior interactions
or external sources; skills organize knowledge into reusable procedures;
tools provide executable operations; and context determines the
information, instructions, and environmental settings available during
execution. Assets self-evolution changes what the agent can recall,
apply, invoke, or condition its reasoning on, with representative
examples including SWE-Exp ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20)), CODESKILL
([Li et al., 2026c](#bib.bib43)), and Live-SWE-agent ([Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)). These components may share content while serving
different functions: knowledge retained in memory can enter the current
context, and a learned procedure can be realized through an executable
tool.

### 3.2 Architecture Self-Evolution

Architecture determines how the agent’s capabilities are organized into
task execution. We describe it through three complementary aspects,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}_{t}=\left(h_{t},w_{t},g_{t}\right),\qquad\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t+1}=\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{A}_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}),
``` |  | (8) |

where $`h_{t}`$ denotes the harness, $`w_{t}`$ the workflow, and
$`g_{t}`$ the multi-agent organization. The harness governs runtime
interaction and execution control; the workflow specifies the
arrangement and dependencies of task-solving stages; and the multi-agent
organization determines how responsibilities and information are
distributed among participating agents. Architecture self-evolution
changes how available capabilities are coordinated, allowing experience
to revise the procedure through which subsequent tasks are solved, as
exemplified by DGM ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib18)), AFlow ([Zhang et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib40)), and EvoMAC ([Hu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib38)).
These architectural aspects are not independent: a change in
collaboration may alter the workflow, while its implementation may
require modifications to the harness. For example, moving validation
ahead of a costly rewrite changes which assumptions reach implementation
without adding a new capability. Requiring a reviewer to inspect an
intermediate result similarly changes a decision rule while leaving the
communication graph fixed. Architecture therefore includes both
structural connections and the rules governing their use. Even a small
edit to these rules can affect many later decisions, making the scope of
the change more informative than its code size.

### 3.3 Model Self-Evolution

Model self-evolution incorporates coding experience into the parameters
underlying action selection. Let $`x`$ denote the information available
at a decision point and $`a`$ an agent action. Parameter adaptation
changes the policy exercised within the surrounding agent system,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}\widetilde{\theta}_{t+1}=\mathcal{U}_{\theta}(\mathcal{A}_{t},\tau_{t},f_{t}),\\
\pi_{\theta_{t}}(a\mid x;\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t})\;\longrightarrow\;\pi_{\widetilde{\theta}_{t+1}}(a\mid x;\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t}).\end{gathered}
``` |  | (9) |

Holding assets and architecture fixed in this expression isolates the
effect of parameter changes without requiring them to remain fixed
throughout evolution. Our taxonomy includes self-play co-evolution,
environment-reward reinforcement learning, and harness co-evolution.
These directions organize learning through coupled task generation and
solving, feedback from environmental interaction, or adaptation between
the model and its runtime harness. Representative approaches include
Self-Play SWE-RL ([Wei et al., 2026b](#bib.bib55)) and Agent-RLVR ([Da
et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)). Their shared target is the learned policy,
through which experience can influence subsequent decisions without
retrieving each contributing experience explicitly.

### 3.4 Research Landscape

We describe the publication landscape of the 108 methods in Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents"),
counting each once by its primary update target. Benchmarks, products,
and separate empirical studies are excluded. First availability follows
arXiv dates for 103 papers and catalogue years for five. The 2026
quarterly view uses arXiv months or documented release quarters for four
papers without arXiv links. Venue labels follow the catalogue and are
kept separate from first availability: 13 papers appeared on arXiv
before their venue year.

Figure
[4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Research Landscape ‣ 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
shows two papers in 2023, six in 2024, 25 in 2025, and 75 in 2026, with
18, 30, and 27 in the first three quarters of 2026. The first half of
2026 alone contains 48 methods, nearly twice the 2025 total, showing
marked acceleration within this corpus. The 2026 entries comprise 37
asset, 32 architecture, and six model updates; across all years, these
categories contain 51, 43, and 14 papers, respectively. Assets and
architecture thus account for 69 of 75 entries in 2026, compared with 17
of 25 in 2025, suggesting growing attention to reusable resources and
editable execution structures. These counts describe research activity
rather than effectiveness. The curated collection and incomplete Q3 also
preclude conclusions about field-wide growth or a slowdown after Q2.

The outlet view records 73 papers as arXiv, 11 as ICLR, six as NeurIPS,
five as ICML, and 13 under other labels. Here, arXiv means no other
venue is recorded; catalogue labels may lag publication. This
distribution describes dissemination at the snapshot date, while Section
[8](#S8 "8 Benchmarks and Evaluation ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
examines evidence of actual improvement.

Figure 4: Publication landscape of 108 methods. (a) First availability
by update target; Q3\* is incomplete as of September 2026. (b) Recorded
outlets; “arXiv” indicates no other listed venue.

The following sections examine the mechanisms and representative work in
assets self-evolution (Section
[4](#S4 "4 Assets Self-Evolution ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")),
architecture self-evolution (Section
[5](#S5 "5 Architecture Self-Evolution ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")),
and model self-evolution (Section
[6](#S6 "6 Model Self-Evolution ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")).

## 4 Assets Self-Evolution

Asset self-evolution turns coding experience and external knowledge into
resources that remain available for subsequent execution. The evolving
state is
$`\mathcal{S}_{t}=(\mathcal{M}_{t},\mathcal{K}_{t},\mathcal{T}_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t})`$.
The main design choices concern the unit of experience retained, its
representation, and the conditions under which it is revised or reused.
Memory can preserve a diagnosis and its supporting evidence; a skill can
organize that knowledge into a procedure; a tool can implement an
operation; and context can expose the information needed at the next
decision point. These roles connect the four asset types while giving
each a distinct update target. Their evolution can involve
consolidation, correction, or removal as well as the addition of new
resources. Table

### 4.1 Memory Self-Evolution

Memory evolution updates $`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ within the asset state
$`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$. Its central design choice is the unit of knowledge
that survives an interaction, together with the conditions under which
it should be recalled. We distinguish experience-derived memory from
external knowledge memory by the provenance of that knowledge. Both
concern explicit storage outside model parameters, but the former
abstracts agent executions, whereas the latter incorporates repository
history or human guidance. For comparison, we represent a memory item as
$`m_{i}=(v_{i},e_{i},\Omega_{i})`$, where $`v_{i}`$ is the retained
knowledge, $`e_{i}`$ its supporting evidence, and $`\Omega_{i}`$ its
applicability conditions. These fields may be explicit metadata or
implicit in the memory text. An agent-derived diagnosis and a
developer-provided convention can share this representation while
drawing on different sources of $`e_{i}`$.

Experience-Derived Memory. The shortest reuse horizon is a later attempt
at the same problem. Reflexion retains verbal interpretations of
feedback in an episodic buffer to guide subsequent trials ([Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib33)). SAGE instead abstracts an initial rollout into
a plan that preserves dependencies and constraints before re-executing
the same task ([Hayashi et al., 2025](#bib.bib65)). SE-Agent revises,
recombines, and refines pilot trajectories, using relationships among
previous attempts to explore alternative solutions ([Lin et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib127)). These methods demonstrate different ways of making
earlier computation useful to later execution. Their same-task
improvements should be distinguished from evidence that a retained
memory benefits unseen tasks, and from improvements obtained simply by
increasing the number of attempts.

Across tasks, abstraction must balance reusable guidance against the
details that make a past solution applicable. SWE-Exp distills
successful and failed repair trajectories into a bank spanning issue
comprehension and concrete code changes ([Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib20)). EvoCoder addresses issue reproduction through a
hierarchical pool separating common experience from repository-specific
experience ([Lin et al., 2024](#bib.bib66)). EXPEREPAIR separates
concrete repair demonstrations from reflective insights in episodic and
semantic memories, combining both when constructing an inference prompt
([Mu et al., 2025](#bib.bib88)). These designs expose complementary
dimensions of memory organization. Repository scope determines where a
lesson applies, while abstraction level determines how much of the
original repair must be reconstructed before it can guide a decision.

Retrieval also needs to match the agent’s current activity. Subtask
Memory aligns storage, retrieval, and updating with functional subtasks,
addressing the mismatch between similar issue descriptions and different
stage-specific reasoning needs ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib68)).
PMCoder couples a phase planner with episodic memory, so the phase
conditions retrieval and memory statistics inform stuck detection and
replanning ([Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib87)). Its matched component
ablations and trajectory analyses connect better state management with
fewer repeated failures. Here the evidence concerns retaining useful
observations during a long repair episode; transferring the mechanism
across backbones does not itself demonstrate transfer of accumulated
memories across issues. Together, these methods suggest that relevance
depends on the decision being made, rather than issue similarity alone.
A relevance-based retrieval rule can make this dependence explicit,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathcal{M}}(x)=\operatorname{Top}_{k_{M}}\!\left(\{m_{i}\in\mathcal{M}_{t}:\Omega_{i}(x)=1\};\,r(m_{i},x)\right),
``` |  | (10) |

where $`x`$ is the current decision state, $`r(m_{i},x)`$ a relevance
score, and $`\operatorname{Top}_{k_{M}}`$ returns up to $`k_{M}`$
highest-scoring eligible items. The condition $`\Omega_{i}(x)=1`$
represents an applicability check, such as a matching repository,
dependency version, or task phase. This is an analytical retrieval rule;
individual methods may implement eligibility and relevance jointly or
use soft scores. It separates the existence of an item in
$`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ from its inclusion in the recalled set
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\mathcal{M}}(x)`$.

Domain-specific feedback further changes what should be remembered.
EvoRepair combines accumulation within a vulnerability with reuse across
vulnerabilities, updating its experience bank through quality-aware
scoring ([Hu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)). MemRepair distinguishes
historical fixes, security patterns, and refinement trajectories,
preserving repository conventions alongside reusable defenses and
lessons from failed validation ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib125)). In
RTL generation, VeriAgent converts simulation and synthesis feedback
into memory nodes with triggering conditions, guidance, and metadata;
its manager inserts, refines, or discards nodes ([Wang et al.,
2026g](#bib.bib124)). The adaptive system for ML library development
retains verified generated programs as demonstrations and selects them
by difficulty, using successful examples to support remaining tasks in
an unfamiliar programming language ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib128)).
These mechanisms retain different evidence, from repair failures to
physical design signals and executable examples, rather than treating
every trajectory as an interchangeable text record.

Memory can also mediate experience sharing and control its own
information cost. ReasoningBank extracts strategies from self-judged
successes and failures, then incorporates new experience after
retrieval-guided execution; its MaTTS extension uses additional
computation to diversify that experience ([Ouyang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib126)). Agent KB shares structured trajectories across
heterogeneous frameworks, combining planning-time retrieval with
feedback-time diagnostic guidance and a disagreement gate ([Tang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27)). PILOT distills procedures and failure modes into
skills and memory during live supervisor–worker execution ([Xiao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib129)). SWE-MeM learns when, what, and how to compress
histories through synthesized training trajectories and memory-aware
GRPO ([Gao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib85)). PILOT couples retained assets
with supervision, while SWE-MeM combines memory management with
parameter learning. Their gains therefore reflect changes beyond memory
contents. More retained experience is not necessarily better. CTIM-Rover
adds general and repository-specific cross-task memories to
AutoCodeRover but does not outperform its baseline in the evaluated
configurations; the authors identify distracting memories and exemplars
as a likely cause ([Lindenbauer et al., 2025](#bib.bib130)). This
negative result makes selective recall part of the improvement
mechanism. Memory may change action selection, giving
$`\delta_{t}(x)>0`$ at some states, without producing a positive
expected gain $`\Delta J_{t}`$. Evaluation should therefore separate
memory quality and retrieval effects from added search, supervision, or
training.

External Knowledge Memory. Repository history records decisions that the
agent did not necessarily make itself. Repository Memory uses historical
commits, linked issues, and summaries of actively changing code regions
to improve localization ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21)). This
supplements a code snapshot with associations between past problems and
likely modification sites. MemCoder structures human commit history into
intent-to-code mappings, refines execution using verification feedback,
and incorporates human-validated solutions into long-term knowledge
([Deng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib86)). The distinction is between recalling
where and why developers changed code and retaining the agent’s own
trial-and-error record, although a single memory system can eventually
contain both. External supervision can also reveal project conventions
that tests do not fully express. Learning to Commit attempts historical
issues, compares its changes with actual commits, and distills the
differences into reusable guidance about style, internal APIs, and
architectural constraints ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib131)). Its
chronological split evaluates future pull requests, directly aligning
the reuse claim with later repository work, although the reported study
centers on one repository. Accumulated Behavioral Rules converts
accepted review comments into persistent instructions and a
pre-submission checklist ([Aggarwal and Ghalaty, 2026](#bib.bib91)). Its
production observations support cross-session retention of corrections,
but the small session sample and absence of a controlled baseline limit
causal claims about improvement. Such artifacts overlap with skills and
context in their eventual use; their distinguishing contribution here is
converting developer knowledge into a maintained source of guidance.

Across both sources, effective memory requires preserving the
relationship between $`v_{i}`$, $`e_{i}`$, and $`\Omega_{i}`$. A compact
description of maintenance is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{t+1}=\bigl(\mathcal{M}_{t}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathcal{M}}\bigr)\cup\mathcal{W}_{t}^{\mathcal{M}},
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{t}`$ contains
entries selected for removal or replacement and
$`\mathcal{W}_{t}^{\mathcal{M}}`$ contains proposed new or revised
entries. Merging several records removes their originals and writes a
consolidated item; retirement removes an item without replacement. The
tilde denotes a candidate state subject to adoption. This representation
allows memory to improve through correction and consolidation even when
$`|\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{t+1}|\leq|\mathcal{M}_{t}|`$. A repository
convention may cease to hold after refactoring, while a general repair
strategy may require different local actions. Consequently, the
evaluation distribution $`\mathcal{D}`$ used to estimate
$`\Delta J_{t}`$ should reflect whether reuse is claimed within an
episode, across issues in one repository, or across repositories. That
alignment determines whether memory has supported local continuity,
accumulated project expertise, or broader transfer.

### 4.2 Skill Self-Evolution

Skill self-evolution turns coding knowledge into reusable guidance for
action, updating the skill collection $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$. A skill
specifies a procedure and the conditions under which it should be
applied, potentially combining instructions with executable resources.
Its contribution therefore depends on more than whether its content
accurately summarizes a past task. The procedure must remain applicable,
be selected when needed, and improve the decisions made by the receiving
agent. Following Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents"),
we examine acquisition, optimization, governance, and safety as
complementary concerns across the skill lifecycle. We write
$`k=(\Omega_{k},p_{k},\mathcal{Q}_{k})`$ for its applicability
conditions, procedure, and resource requirements, respectively. The
requirements $`\mathcal{Q}_{k}`$ can identify tools, dependencies, or
other skills needed to execute $`p_{k}`$.

Skill Acquisition. Acquisition begins with choosing the experience from
which a procedure can be abstracted. A candidate
$`\widetilde{k}=\operatorname{Distill}(\tau_{t},f_{t};\mathcal{K}_{t})`$
captures a proposed procedure together with its conditions and
requirements; conditioning on $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$ allows the distiller
to account for existing guidance. CODESKILL ([Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib43)) learns a management policy that extracts task-level
procedures and event-driven responses from coding trajectories. It
combines rubric feedback with the incremental execution benefit of
generated skills for a frozen downstream agent, and checks whether the
trajectory follows the supplied guidance. This connects acquisition to
the earlier distinction between subsequent use and behavioral
contribution. Socratic-SWE ([Xiao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib45)) gives
extracted skills a different role. Its registry summarizes recurring
failures and effective repairs to guide the synthesis of verifiable
repository tasks, which then train the Solver. Skills thus influence
future behavior through curriculum construction as well as through
direct instructions, illustrating interaction between asset and model
evolution.

Repository-specific methods can actively generate the experience they
need. GSkill ([Tan et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)) combines SWE-smith tasks
with reflective evolutionary optimization of repository skill documents,
evaluating candidate guidance through agent rollouts. SkillForge ([Chen
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib132)) instead creates practice issues by
reimplementing test-covered repository functionality, then distills the
resulting solutions into skills associated with repository entities.
Both use a repository as a source of practice, but their retained
guidance differs in how it is organized for later use. Broader reuse
also requires compatibility with skills already acquired. GSE ([Yang et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib89)) maintains a Skill Relation Graph, consolidates
related local updates, and uses replay verification to limit overfitting
and regression. Acquiring a useful procedure therefore includes deciding
how its scope and relationships fit the existing collection.

Hardware coding exposes the importance of the available verifier.
Verilog-Evolve ([Pei et al., 2026](#bib.bib133)) derives modular
guidance from logged refinement histories, with creation, improvement,
or skipping informed by verifier reports. Simulation, synthesis, and
timing proxies provide distinct evidence about what a useful procedure
must preserve. Trace2Skill ([Du and Pinckney, 2026](#bib.bib134)) uses
an oracle, mutator, and selector loop to turn rollout failures into
task-specific skills for later search, editing, validation, and
recovery. Its bounded dense verifier feedback provides diagnostic
observations while withholding hidden harnesses and reference solutions.
The two approaches emphasize cross-session accumulation and test-time
adaptation, respectively, so their reuse claims require different
evaluation scopes. Representation also affects whether the acquired
knowledge becomes actionable. *From Procedural Skills to Strategy Genes*
([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib135)) finds in scientific code-solving
experiments that compact control-oriented representations and distilled
failure warnings can outperform expanded documentation packages. More
detailed recollection need not yield more effective procedural guidance.

Skill Optimization. Optimization concerns both the quality of procedures
and the way they are selected and applied. To isolate a skill
collection’s contribution, let $`\mathcal{A}_{t}[\mathcal{K}]`$ denote
the agent with its skill collection replaced by $`\mathcal{K}`$ and all
other components held fixed. Define
$`G_{t}(\mathcal{K})=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}[s(\mathcal{A}_{t}[\mathcal{K}],q;B)]`$
using the same evaluation distribution and execution budget as before,
with the expectation also averaging over execution randomness. A
candidate’s marginal gain is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{t}^{\mathcal{K}}(k\mid\mathcal{K})=G_{t}(\mathcal{K}\cup\{k\})-G_{t}(\mathcal{K}).
``` |  | (12) |

For a revision, $`\mathcal{K}`$ excludes the version being replaced, so
the old and new versions can be assessed against the same base
collection. A skill’s utility depends on this base; overlap, conflict,
or complementarity can make its contribution differ from its standalone
performance. EffiSkill ([Wang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib67)) mines concrete
Operator Skills and higher-level Meta Skills from slow/fast program
pairs, then combines diagnosis, retrieval, and planning to optimize
unseen programs without runtime feedback. Its offline library provides a
comparison point for systems that continually revise skills during
execution. daVinci-kernel ([Fu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib137)) closes that
loop for GPU kernels, jointly training skill selection, kernel
generation, and skill summarization on a shared model backbone. New
skills enter its library only after execution confirms reproducible
speedups. Its improvements therefore involve both an evolving skill
collection and parameter adaptation, requiring care when attributing
gains to $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$ alone.

The optimization objective also matters. SkillMOO ([Gong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib136)) evolves skill bundles using LLM-proposed edits and
Pareto selection over task success and inference cost. Such a tradeoff
can be expressed through the nondominated candidate collections

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathfrak{P}_{t}=\operatorname{ParetoMax}_{\mathcal{K}\in\mathfrak{C}_{t}}\bigl(G_{t}(\mathcal{K}),-\operatorname{Cost}_{t}(\mathcal{K})\bigr),
``` |  | (13) |

where $`\mathfrak{C}_{t}`$ is the set of candidate collections and
$`\operatorname{Cost}_{t}`$ measures their average execution cost under
the common budget cap $`B`$. A collection is nondominated if no
candidate is at least as good on both objectives and strictly better on
one. This formulation allows several useful tradeoffs instead of
imposing a single performance–cost weight. SkillMOO’s analysis finds
pruning and substitution prominent among successful edits, showing that
improvement can come from reducing guidance. Specialization likewise
needs evidence of future relevance. *Do Personalized Skills Help Coding
Agents?* ([Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib92)) extracts developer
preferences from interaction histories, but reports small, inconsistent
improvements from personalization in simulator-based replay, while
pooled generic skills yield more consistent gains. Together, these
studies suggest that optimization should match procedural specificity
and cost to the intended reuse distribution $`\mathcal{D}`$, rather than
assume that longer or more personalized skills are better.

Skill Governance. Governance determines which skills remain available as
a collection grows. For an existing skill $`k\in\mathcal{K}_{t}`$, its
removal contribution is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\gamma_{t}(k)=G_{t}(\mathcal{K}_{t})-G_{t}(\mathcal{K}_{t}\setminus\{k\}).
``` |  | (14) |

A small or negative estimate of $`\gamma_{t}(k)`$ motivates review for
redundancy or retirement. The score remains conditional on the other
skills and the evaluation distribution; it does not establish that $`k`$
is useless in every setting. Both $`\gamma_{t}(k)`$ and
$`\Delta_{t}^{\mathcal{K}}`$ require estimates from comparable
executions, making evaluation uncertainty part of governance. SkillsVote
([Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib138)) links collection and recommendation
to post-execution attribution. It profiles environment requirements and
verifiability, searches structured skill folders, and separates
skill-guided subtasks from agent exploration and environmental effects
before admitting reusable discoveries. Ratchet ([Zhang et al.,
2026j](#bib.bib90)) focuses on retirement, combining measured
contribution with a bounded active library and constrained synthesis.
Its analysis distinguishes judge errors that increase sampling
requirements from false-positive judgments that can disable retirement
under the analyzed rule. A governance policy thus depends on the
reliability of the evidence used to retain or remove skills.

*Who Grades the Grader?* ([Zhang et al., 2026k](#bib.bib139)) makes this
dependence explicit by evolving inspectable evaluation functions
alongside the skill library. Anchored reference judgments constrain the
evaluator, while its agreement with hidden ground truth is checked
separately. Removing these anchors can produce an always-pass evaluator
even when downstream scores appear satisfactory. This extends the
adoption decision for $`\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_{t+1}`$ to the criterion
governing adoption itself. Improving skills and validating their
evaluator are related but distinct requirements, particularly when
execution does not supply a complete oracle.

Skill Safety. Persistence can amplify errors as well as useful
experience. *Library Drift* ([Zhang et al., 2026i](#bib.bib1)) diagnoses
how unrestricted accumulation degrades retrieval and introduces
irrelevant guidance. Its contribution logs, outcome-based retirement,
and active-library cap make degradation observable and governable. *When
Self-Evolution Backfires* ([Shang et al., 2026](#bib.bib140)) identifies
a further propagation mechanism. Defective skills can influence the
distillation of later skills, so removing the original entry leaves
contaminated descendants. Its Verifier-as-Gatekeeper screens structural
validity, behavioral harmlessness, and semantic consistency, then
selects skill subsets by marginal gain before admission. Control must
therefore cover individual skills and their interactions within the
collection. An illustrative admission rule for a candidate $`k`$
combines estimated benefit with specified checks,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{Admit}_{t}(k)=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\widehat{\Delta}_{t}^{\mathcal{K}}(k\mid\mathcal{K}_{t})>\epsilon\right]\mathbf{1}\!\left[\operatorname{Check}_{t}(k,\mathcal{K}_{t})=1\right],
``` |  | (15) |

where $`\mathbf{1}[\cdot]`$ is an indicator, $`\epsilon\geq 0`$ a gain
threshold, and $`\operatorname{Check}_{t}`$ represents the chosen
validity, compatibility, and safety checks. The hat marks an empirical
gain estimate. For a replacement, the gain compares the new and old
versions against the same base collection. This rule expresses a
conservative admission policy; passing finite checks remains evidence
under those checks, rather than a guarantee of safety in all future
uses.

EVOMAL ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib141)) demonstrates an adversarial
counterpart in coding agents. A retrieved malicious skill can become an
authoring template, causing harmful content to be copied into newly
stored and executed skills. Agent-authored descendants can persist after
the planted entries are removed; the proposed counter-prompt reduces
copying-based self-poisoning in the evaluated setting. These findings
make provenance and admission consequential throughout evolution. In
terms of the five links introduced earlier, a contaminated update can
survive retention, influence subsequent behavior, and generate the
evidence for further updates. Safe skill evolution must therefore assess
both immediate behavior and the content that a skill helps propagate
into future versions of $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$.

### 4.3 Tool Self-Evolution

Tool self-evolution updates the executable utilities in
$`\mathcal{T}_{t}`$. Where a skill describes a procedure, a tool
provides a callable implementation. The retained update is a utility or
adapter that supports subsequent execution, rather than the project code
delivered for the current task.

Live-SWE-agent interleaves issue resolution with tool creation and
revision within a minimal bash-based agent ([Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)). Reflection on environment feedback prompts the agent
to build utilities for editing, code search, or specialized analysis,
then invoke and refine them as the task proceeds. Its main reuse scope
is later steps within the same issue, illustrating how execution
experience can expand available operations without an offline evolution
phase.

SIGA evolves a simulator-facing adapter around a fixed coding model and
execution loop ([Ho et al., 2026](#bib.bib98)). An offline proposer uses
prior trajectories and rewards to revise the task primer, procedural
memory, and auxiliary skills, retaining candidates selected by
validation performance. These updates span several assets. Its main
evolved comparison disables skill invocation to keep the runtime tool
configuration fixed, so the gains support improved adapter contents
rather than newly added tools. Together, the two methods distinguish
expanding executable operations from improving their domain interface.
In either case, a working utility alone does not establish a positive
downstream gain $`\Delta J_{t}`$.

### 4.4 Context Self-Evolution

Context self-evolution targets $`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$, the information,
instructions, and environmental settings through which an agent
encounters a coding task. The reusable change may be selected repository
evidence, a compression rule, an optimized prompt, or a repository-side
information structure. These changes shape what reaches the decision
process and how it is presented. The central distinction is between
constructing context for one invocation and retaining an
experience-informed change that influences subsequent execution. The
methods below occupy different points along this boundary and support
different scopes of reuse.

Context Retrieval. Retrieval evolves when execution changes the evidence
available to later queries or the way relevant evidence is assembled.
EVOR synchronously updates queries and a heterogeneous knowledge base
containing documentation, web content, code snippets, and execution
feedback ([Su et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)). Generated programs or their
error messages enter the retrieval pool, so later attempts can condition
on evidence produced by earlier execution. Its loop retains more than a
revised answer, although successful execution of a retrieved snippet
does not establish its semantic correctness. CodeMEM addresses
continuity across iterative repository-level generation ([Wang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib3)). It uses AST structure to preserve relevant code
context, incorporates newly retrieved blocks when needed, and maintains
code-centric session memory to detect forgotten corrections. Its
context-retrieval role overlaps with memory because retention supplies
the evidence from which later context is assembled. These methods
illustrate reuse within an evolving interaction; their reported gains
should not automatically be interpreted as transfer to unrelated
repositories. To distinguish retained assets from their use at a
decision point, let $`\mathcal{B}_{t}`$ be the available evidence pool,
$`p_{t}(x)`$ the instructions for state $`x`$, and $`\phi_{t}`$ the
selection or compression mechanism. These are components of the retained
context assets $`\mathcal{C}_{t}`$. The assembled context can be written
as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}c_{t}(x)=\operatorname{Assemble}\!\left(p_{t}(x),\phi_{t}(\operatorname{Retrieve}(x,\mathcal{B}_{t});x)\right),\\
|c_{t}(x)|_{\mathrm{tok}}\leq L.\end{gathered}
``` |  | (16) |

The lowercase $`c_{t}(x)`$ denotes one constructed context and $`L`$ its
token budget. Updating $`\mathcal{B}_{t}`$, $`p_{t}`$, or $`\phi_{t}`$
changes what later constructions can draw on. A different $`c_{t}(x)`$
produced from unchanged assets can instead reflect a different query or
task state. This distinction locates the retained update underlying a
context-adaptation claim.

Context Compression. Compression determines which observations remain
visible when terminal output or repository content exceeds the useful
context budget. TACO discovers and refines structured filtering rules
from terminal trajectories, pairing applicability conditions with
retention and removal patterns ([Ren et al., 2026a](#bib.bib84)).
Effective rules are written back to a global pool and selected for later
tasks, making the compression behavior itself reusable. SWE-Pruner
instead conditions a trained neural skimmer on an explicit goal supplied
by the coding agent and selects relevant source lines ([Wang et al.,
2026i](#bib.bib95)). It demonstrates task-adaptive context selection,
but adaptation of the selected lines does not by itself establish
continual updating of the skimmer from deployment experience. This
distinction separates TACO’s retained rule evolution from the
application of a learned compression component. For an original context
$`c_{t}(x)`$ with nonzero token length and its compressed version
$`c^{\prime}_{t}(x)`$, the fractional token reduction is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{t}(x)=1-\frac{|c^{\prime}_{t}(x)|_{\mathrm{tok}}}{|c_{t}(x)|_{\mathrm{tok}}}.
``` |  | (17) |

A positive $`\rho_{t}(x)`$ indicates token savings, but can coexist with
$`\Delta J_{t}<0`$ if compression removes information needed for correct
action. Comparisons should therefore consider both token reduction and
downstream performance under a common budget. The relevant tradeoff
depends on which observations are removed, as well as their volume.

Prompt Evolution. Prompt updates change the instructions conditioning a
frozen code generator. For a problem prompt $`p_{q}`$, writing
$`p^{\prime}_{q}=r_{t}(p_{q})`$ separates the revised prompt instance
$`p^{\prime}_{q}`$ from the transformation rule $`r_{t}`$. The instance
may be reused in another attempt at $`q`$, whereas $`r_{t}`$ can be
applied to prompts for other problems if its conditions hold. EPiC
evolves variants of a problem prompt, using the test performance of
generated code to guide selection ([Taherkhani et al.,
2024](#bib.bib4)). It illustrates feedback-driven prompt search within a
problem, without requiring a durable instruction shared across problems.
Reinforcement-learning-based prompt optimization learns a PPO policy
that chooses among direct generation, lexical mutation, and semantic
rewriting using unit-test rewards ([Esfahani et al.,
2026](#bib.bib142)). Here, the generator remains frozen, while the
optimizer learns how to produce the context updates. SePO moves reuse to
the system-prompt level, evolving both task-agent prompts and the prompt
agent’s own instructions through an archive of candidates ([Tao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib5)). The reusable artifact thus includes guidance for
performing further prompt optimization. From Failing to Passing evolves
natural-language transformation rules and combines them with
execution-feedback repair in DUALFIX ([Akli et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)).
Its cross-problem reuse and cross-model transfer tests examine whether
an effective transformation generalizes beyond the failures used to
discover it. These approaches distinguish an improved prompt instance
from a reusable prompt-transformation mechanism, an important difference
when defining the evaluation distribution $`\mathcal{D}`$.

Environment Evolution. The agent’s information surface can also change
on the repository side. Libra introduces hierarchical Markdown catalogs
and rewrites them after a frozen solver fails to localize information in
response to synthetic queries ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)). The
catalogs persist as navigable indices for later queries and solvers. Its
transfer experiments across models and problem sets test whether the
improved environment remains useful beyond the optimization
interactions. EvoEnv explores a different environmental target,
synthesizing reusable Python environments that generate reasoning
instances, compute references, and score answers ([Shi et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib144)). Candidates enter an active training pool after
validity, semantic consistency, difficulty, and novelty checks, and the
shared generator–solver policy is updated through reinforcement
learning. This is environment–model co-evolution for reasoning training,
rather than repository configuration or direct evidence of improved
software issue resolution. The comparison identifies two distinct reuse
channels. Libra changes what future solvers can navigate, whereas EvoEnv
changes the executable sources of future training experience. Their
common asset-level feature is a retained environment artifact, while the
downstream learning mechanisms and the claims supported by evaluation
differ. For a pool $`\mathfrak{E}_{t}`$ of retained task-generating
environments, their effect on training can be represented by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{train}}=\sum_{e\in\mathfrak{E}_{t}}\alpha_{t}(e)\mathcal{D}_{e},
``` |  | (18) |

where $`\mathcal{D}_{e}`$ is the task distribution generated by
environment $`e`$, $`\alpha_{t}(e)\geq 0`$, and
$`\sum_{e}\alpha_{t}(e)=1`$. Revising environments or their sampling
weights changes the experience available for subsequent learning. This
abstraction applies to generative training environments such as EvoEnv;
repository catalogs such as Libra instead change the evidence available
to the solver on an existing task. Environment adaptation can thus
influence either the information used during execution or the
distribution from which future learning experience is obtained.

Across these four asset types, the common challenge is to preserve
useful experience in a form that can influence the right later decision.
Memory emphasizes the evidence retained, skills the procedures made
reusable, tools the operations made executable, and context the
information exposed during execution. An asset may be present while
$`\delta_{t}(x)=0`$ at a given state. Even when $`\delta_{t}(x)>0`$,
improvement requires separate evidence that $`\Delta J_{t}>0`$ over the
intended scope of reuse. Comparisons should therefore isolate the
contribution of retained assets from additional search, training, or
feedback, and account for their maintenance costs and failure modes.

## 5 Architecture Self-Evolution

Architecture self-evolution incorporates coding experience into the
mechanisms that organize execution. Within
$`\mathcal{H}_{t}=(h_{t},w_{t},g_{t})`$, an update may change runtime
control in the harness, dependencies among workflow stages, or the
allocation of responsibilities and information among agents. These
targets offer different ways to address the same failure. A missed
validation step may motivate a submission check in the harness, an
earlier testing stage in the workflow, or a revised handoff to a
reviewing agent. The resulting improvement can come from arranging
existing capabilities more effectively, even when the available tools
and model parameters remain unchanged. The distinction concerns the
functional role of the update, since a workflow or collaboration change
may also require harness code. Following Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents"),
we examine how experience becomes a retained execution rule,
task-solving structure, or coordination mechanism.

### 5.1 Harness Evolution

Harness evolution updates the executable layer $`h_{t}`$ that mediates
model interaction, tool execution, feedback handling, and termination.
In practice, harness optimization may also revise prompts, memory,
skills, and tools in $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$. We classify changes to
reusable content or available operations as asset updates, and changes
to execution organization and control as architecture updates. A method
can combine both, so gains from an evolved harness should be interpreted
in light of the components actually modified.

Updating execution control gives experience a direct route into agent
behavior. A debugging lesson stored as a skill still depends on
retrieval and the agent’s decision to follow it; a harness intervention
can check its activating condition whenever execution reaches the
relevant point. Its influence therefore depends on where it is
installed, which states activate it, and what it changes when activated.
Its key opportunity is to convert a recurring failure into an
intervention at the point where that failure arises. For example, a
repeated invalid tool call may motivate argument validation before
execution, while an unproductive retry loop may motivate a recovery rule
after feedback. To make this intervention explicit, let $`z`$ be the
runtime state, including execution history and remaining budget, and let
$`b`$ be a control decision such as dispatching a call, retrying, or
terminating. A harness induces a transition kernel

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(b,z^{\prime})\sim P_{h_{t}}(\cdot\mid z;\mathcal{S}_{t},\theta_{t}),\qquad\widetilde{h}_{t+1}=\operatorname{Apply}(h_{t},e_{t}),
``` |  | (19) |

where $`e_{t}`$ is a proposed code or configuration edit and
$`z^{\prime}`$ is the resulting runtime state. This description locates
the update in the rules governing execution, without prescribing how a
method must search for edits. The six mechanisms below emphasize
different aspects of that search and can coexist within one system.

Archive-Based Evolution. An archive makes earlier executable agents
available as starting points for further improvement. This matters
because a modification can have value beyond its immediate task score. A
branch that currently performs poorly may contain a useful
implementation choice, expose a recurring failure, or support a later
change that would be difficult to discover from the current best agent.
DGM operationalizes this idea by sampling agents from an expanding
archive, modifying their source code, and evaluating the resulting
variants on coding tasks ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib18)). Retaining
alternative branches allows search to continue from earlier designs
instead of requiring every useful path to pass through the latest agent.
The archive retains executable implementations alongside their traces,
evaluation records, and lineage information. Search uses this history
both to select a parent and to construct a candidate modification.
Retention for further search and adoption for task execution are
separate decisions. An archive can preserve an informative candidate
without making it the deployed agent.

Choosing a parent raises a different question from choosing an agent to
solve the next task. Huxley GM identifies a mismatch between current
coding performance and the ability to produce useful descendants, and
uses estimated clade-level metaproductivity to guide tree search ([Wang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib48)). To express this distinction independently
of a particular estimator, let
$`u(\mathcal{A})=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}[s(\mathcal{A},q;B)]`$
measure current performance. Under a specified search protocol and
current archive $`\mathcal{Z}_{t}`$, let
$`\operatorname{Desc}_{C}(\mathcal{A})`$ be the random set of
descendants generated from $`\mathcal{A}`$ with evolution budget $`C`$.
A conceptual measure of its value as a starting point is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Psi_{t}(\mathcal{A};C)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\in\{\mathcal{A}\}\cup\operatorname{Desc}_{C}(\mathcal{A})}u(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})\;\middle|\;\mathcal{Z}_{t}\right].
``` |  | (20) |

The evolution budget $`C`$ pays for candidate construction and
assessment, whereas $`B`$ controls each agent’s task execution. A high
$`u(\mathcal{A})`$ need not imply a high $`\Psi_{t}(\mathcal{A};C)`$.
The latter depends on which descendants the search can reach and afford
to evaluate. It is an idealized quantity; observed descendant results
provide evidence for estimating such potential. This distinction
explains why selecting only the current highest-scoring parent can
discard useful routes to improvement.

Mendel GM focuses on what evidence should inform the next modification.
Its reaction-norm mutation compares one agent’s trajectories across
tasks, while cross-lineage hybridization uses another lineage’s
trajectory on the same task ([Anonymous, 2026](#bib.bib47)). These
comparisons reveal different information. Repeated failures across tasks
can suggest a recurring weakness in the harness; different outcomes on a
shared task can suggest a strategy worth transferring. Writing
$`\mathcal{E}_{i,q}`$ for an agent–task execution record and
$`\Omega_{t}`$ for the observed agent–task pairs, the two evidence views
are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\mathrm{tasks}}(i)=\{\mathcal{E}_{i,q}:(i,q)\in\Omega_{t}\},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{t}^{\mathrm{agents}}(q)=\{\mathcal{E}_{j,q}:(j,q)\in\Omega_{t}\}.
``` |  | (21) |

The first holds the agent fixed, and the second holds the task fixed.
Neither requires every agent to run on every task. These views turn the
archive into a source of comparative diagnoses as well as candidate
implementations. Executing the modified agent under matched conditions
tests these proposed explanations.

The archive also creates an allocation problem because evaluating every
possible modification can consume the evolution budget before useful
branches are explored. SIFT uses an LLM judge to rank candidate patches
and concentrates expensive benchmark execution on promising candidates
([Fu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib63)). By reducing full evaluations,
screening can make a wider search affordable, but its usefulness depends
on which candidates it excludes. A judge that repeatedly favors familiar
edits can suppress the unusual branches that archive-based exploration
is intended to retain. The relevant comparison therefore concerns the
quality of agents discovered under a common evolution budget, alongside
the cost and reliability of candidate screening.

The proposal and evaluation mechanisms can themselves evolve.
HyperAgents places the task agent and its modifying meta agent in one
editable program, allowing experience to revise both task execution and
the procedure producing future updates ([Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib146)). By modifying the proposal mechanism itself,
improvement can change which modifications become reachable. RQGM also
