````math
permits evaluator changes between epochs while keeping the utility fixed
within each epoch ([Iacob et al., 2026](#bib.bib145)). If the internal
objective changes from $`u_{t}`$ to $`u_{t+1}`$, a higher reported score
can reflect both a different agent and a different criterion. Comparison
under the common $`\mathcal{D}`$, $`s`$, and $`B`$ remains necessary to
interpret the result as $`\Delta J_{t}`$. Across these methods, the
archive’s contribution depends on how retained variants change parent
selection, comparative diagnosis, proposal generation, or allocation of
evaluation effort. Its size alone does not capture that contribution.

Iteration-Based Evolution. Iterative methods make the agent’s
implementation a recurring coding task. SICA uses reflection and editing
tools to revise the program orchestrating its model calls and actions,
retaining code changes for later executions ([Robeyns et al.,
2025](#bib.bib46)). STOP makes this relationship explicit through a seed
program improver that applies its own language-model-assisted search to
itself, changing how subsequent programs are generated and selected
while leaving model weights fixed ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib64)).
Ouroboros extends implementation revision into continued operation.
Explicit improvement tasks and problems encountered during ordinary work
produce reviewed commits that become the runtime for later work
([Razzhigaev et al., 2026](#bib.bib106)). Its frozen benchmark snapshots
and live deployment lineage provide different evidence, respectively
about a particular system version and the operation of a continuing
update process. The defining transition is adoption into later
execution; repeatedly editing candidate code does not establish that
this transition occurred.

Iterative revision also couples the quality of the current agent to the
quality of its future edits. A change that improves repository
inspection may help both ordinary issue resolution and inspection of the
agent’s own implementation. However, these two uses expose different
failure cases. Evaluating later self-modification attempts can reveal
whether an update improves the revision process as well as the task
solver. Retaining versioned implementations makes this distinction
inspectable and supports returning to an earlier revision when a later
change degrades execution.

Trace-Driven Evolution. Execution traces can reveal which runtime
mechanism prevented an agent from using its available capabilities
effectively. Self-Harness clusters recurring failures, proposes small
changes tied to those failures, and retains modifications through
regression testing ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib97)). AHE makes
editable components observable at file level, condenses trajectories
into inspectable evidence, and pairs edits with predictions that can be
checked against subsequent outcomes ([Lin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib74)).
HarnessFix provides more explicit localization by aligning runtime data
and control flow with harness artifacts, then converting recurring
diagnoses into scoped repair specifications ([Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib75)). AutoSaddler combines mini-batch diagnosis and
structured patching with development-set selection and separate final
testing, distinguishing repair of observed failures from evidence that
an update generalizes ([Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib147)). ReCreate uses
experience retrieval and a reasoning–creation process to generate
scaffold edits, abstracting individual interactions into reusable domain
patterns ([Hao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib148)). Across these methods, the
important conversion is from an observed failure to an actionable
hypothesis about the execution mechanism responsible for it.

A diagnosis becomes operational only when it specifies where and under
what conditions execution should change. AHE illustrates this with an
intervention that records protected output paths after successful
validation and intercepts later commands that would delete or reset
those outputs ([Lin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib74)). HarnessFix retains both
applicability and non-applicability conditions with repair outcomes,
helping later edits respect the scope of earlier experience ([Chen et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib75)). To describe this class of local change, let
$`z`$ include the runtime state and pending decision at a chosen
intervention point. An intended guarded transformation can be written as

|     |                                               |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       I_{e}(z)=\begin{cases}R_{e}(z),&g_{e}(z)=1,\\
       z,&g_{e}(z)=0,\end{cases}
       ```                                            |     | (22) |

where $`g_{e}`$ is the activating condition and $`R_{e}`$ applies the
intended correction before execution continues. This abstraction makes
applicability part of the update rather than an assumption that every
failure-derived rule should apply globally. It also exposes two failure
modes. A correct repair can be ineffective because its condition rarely
activates, or harmful because that condition captures states where the
original behavior was appropriate. Self-Harness addresses a related
decision at proposal time by selecting evidence-supported mechanisms
that its editable surfaces can address, then testing candidates for
regressions ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib97)). Proposal eligibility,
runtime activation, and candidate admission thus govern different parts
of the improvement process.

The resulting updates need not have identical scope. One Recipe, Many
Harnesses finds that a shared evolution procedure yields both
transferable strategies and adaptations specific to language ecosystems
and model weaknesses ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib83)). Evo-Harness
compiles single-shot executions into general and topic-specific skill
guidance that is retrieved for later tasks ([Wei et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib78)). Although described as harness learning, its
retained Markdown skills primarily update procedural assets under our
functional distinction. Harness-of-Harness illustrates a further
boundary by organizing existing harnesses into repeated planning,
implementation, and independent testing, retaining project histories to
inform subsequent development ([Yan et al., 2026](#bib.bib149)). Its
demonstrated progression concerns the software project and accumulated
project state; this does not by itself establish persistent revision of
the underlying execution architecture. These cases make the update
target essential to interpretation, even when methods share the language
of harness improvement.

Population-Based Search. Maintaining several candidates allows
discoveries from different workloads or search paths to inform
subsequent harnesses. DarwinX uses a frozen model and selects harness
variants under a preserve-and-extend criterion, retaining alternative
lineages for recombination ([Zhang et al., 2026l](#bib.bib104)).
HarnessBank organizes successful harnesses by semantic characteristics
in a gene bank, then recombines and screens offspring through staged
verification ([Luo et al., 2026](#bib.bib103)). EvolveNet distributes a
shared harness to deployments with local workloads and combines the
resulting program adaptations using their scopes and supporting
evidence, without centralizing the raw workloads ([Nie et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib79)). HarnessCompass instead emphasizes task-agnostic
edit constraints, feedback from the executing agent, and separate
component optimization before consolidation ([Zhang et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib77)). ADAS provides an earlier code-based search
formulation in which a meta-agent programs new agent designs using an
expanding archive of prior discoveries ([Hu et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib150)). These methods overlap with archive-based
evolution, emphasizing the selection and combination of useful changes
across candidates.

Combining useful changes introduces a further problem of compatibility.
Two edits that each help their original parent may conflict when placed
in one harness, for example if they change the same retry rule or assume
different representations of execution state. Population diversity is
valuable when it preserves complementary solutions and the evidence
needed to reconcile them. The unit of inheritance therefore matters,
whether a method transfers a complete harness, a component
implementation, or a scoped program change. Evaluating these units only
in isolation can miss failures created by their composition.

Pipeline-Driven Evolution. An explicit development pipeline separates
proposing a modification from releasing the resulting agent.
Meta-Harness gives its proposer filesystem access to earlier candidate
code, scores, and execution traces, preserving detailed evidence for
subsequent harness edits ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib99)). AgentDevel
maintains a canonical release line, translating observed failure
symptoms into executable diagnoses and assessing candidates through
newly solved cases and regressions ([Zhang, 2026](#bib.bib151)). CCA
uses a meta-agent to construct, test, and refine agents on a modular
SDK, complementing its runtime orchestration and persistent notes ([Wong
et al., 2025](#bib.bib80)). HarnessX composes typed harness primitives
and evolves them from traces; its broader framework also turns
trajectories into model-training signals, connecting architecture and
model updates ([Chen et al., 2026d](#bib.bib102)). Autogenesis separates
versioned resources from the protocol for proposing, assessing, and
committing changes, with lineage and rollback spanning several component
types ([Zhang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib152)). SEA places admission gates
with anytime-valid certificates around a versioned harness and steering
adapter, with guarantees tied to the gate’s statistical assumptions and
error budget ([Sengupta, 2026](#bib.bib82)). Across these systems, the
pipeline determines which evidence is available when a candidate becomes
persistent.

A release pipeline also preserves the link between a modification and
the evidence used to accept it. Retaining a candidate’s source version,
motivating traces, predicted effects, and evaluation conditions makes
later regressions easier to diagnose. This becomes especially useful
when improvements accumulate across rounds, because a failure may result
from an interaction between accepted edits. Tests of whether the
modified harness runs successfully and measurements of whether it
improves downstream decisions answer different questions. A release
decision benefits from both, together with evidence about which earlier
successes were lost.

Regression-sensitive admission can be expressed using a fixed, nonempty
validation set $`\mathcal{V}`$. Let $`y(h,q)\in\{0,1\}`$ record whether
the agent with harness $`h`$ solves case $`q`$ under matched evaluation
conditions. For a candidate $`\widetilde{h}`$, the fractions of newly
solved and newly failed cases are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F^{+}(\widetilde{h},h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{1}[y(h,q)=0,\ y(\widetilde{h},q)=1],\qquad F^{-}(\widetilde{h},h)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{1}[y(h,q)=1,\ y(\widetilde{h},q)=0].
``` |  | (23) |

The empirical success-rate change is $`F^{+}-F^{-}`$. Reporting both
terms reveals whether an aggregate gain hides losses on previously
solved cases. These are finite-set diagnostics; stochastic outcomes
require repeated evaluation, and passing an admission gate does not
establish benefit beyond its validation scope.

Runtime Evolution. TTHE updates harnesses during evaluation using
unlabeled execution traces, maintaining candidates and committing a
program through execution-derived proxy signals so that it governs
subsequent inputs ([Nie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib76)). Argus retains
verified runtime state, including reusable procedures and routing
decisions, across bounded missions with a fixed model; its longitudinal
evidence is observational rather than a controlled learning ablation
([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib81)). Life-Harness offers a complementary
runtime interface design. It converts training-trajectory failures into
interventions for interface contracts, procedures, action validation,
and recovery, then keeps the resulting harness fixed on unseen tasks
([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib100)). Its evaluation concerns deterministic
interactive environments beyond coding. These cases separate when an
intervention operates from when it is learned. A runtime check can be
the product of offline evolution, while online evolution requires an
update that persists beyond the execution that generated it.

Online updating further couples learning to the changing distribution of
experience. An adopted retry or termination rule changes which states
later executions visit, and therefore which failures the next update can
observe. The absence of an earlier error may indicate a successful
repair, or simply that the revised harness no longer reaches the
relevant situation. Runtime evaluation should therefore track both task
outcomes and the circumstances in which interventions activate. In terms
of the earlier five links, harness evolution must connect a diagnosed
failure to an executable change, its actual activation, and evidence of
benefit over the intended reuse scope.

### 5.2 Workflow Evolution

Workflow evolution updates $`w_{t}`$, the arrangement of task-solving
stages and their dependencies. Its value lies in changing when evidence
becomes available and which decisions it can influence. Moving
validation before an expensive rewrite can expose a mistaken assumption
before it propagates into code; routing a failing test back to
localization can reopen a decision that a fixed repair loop would leave
unchanged. Such changes can improve the use of existing capabilities. We
describe a workflow as $`w_{t}=(V_{t}^{w},E_{t}^{w},\ell_{t})`$, where
$`V_{t}^{w}`$ contains stages, $`E_{t}^{w}`$ describes control and
information dependencies, and $`\ell_{t}`$ assigns instructions and
operations. A proposed structural or configuration edit $`\eta_{t}`$
produces

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widetilde{w}_{t+1}=\operatorname{Edit}(w_{t};\eta_{t}).
       ```                                                       |     | (24) |

Edits can add or remove stages, redirect dependencies, or change branch
and loop conditions. A workflow can therefore evolve by removing
redundant work or improving feedback routing as well as by adding new
stages.

Structure Search and Diagnosis. AFlow searches code-represented
workflows using Monte Carlo Tree Search, reusable operators, execution
feedback, and experience from previous modifications ([Zhang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib40)). Its search explores alternative arrangements of
operations, making the task-solving procedure itself a candidate for
evaluation. SEW separately evolves workflow structure and agent prompts,
including mutation prompts, and studies how textual representations
affect workflow validity ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). These methods
highlight two coupled choices, the structure to execute and the
representation through which that structure can be modified. A search
space must make useful changes expressible while preserving executable
dependencies. JUDGEFLOW addresses where to edit. Its judge inspects
traces, ranks the responsibility of logic blocks, and directs the
optimizer toward problematic blocks ([Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib155)).
This is useful because the stage reporting a failure may have inherited
an earlier mistake. For example, a debugging stage may repeatedly revise
a patch when the underlying problem is incorrect file localization.
Trace-based diagnosis can suggest changing the upstream stage or the
feedback path. The diagnosis guides a proposal; executing the revised
workflow tests whether that proposal improves the overall procedure.

Diversity and Reusable Workflow Components. EvoFlow maintains
heterogeneous workflows through tag-based parent retrieval, crossover,
mutation, and niching selection ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib153)).
Retaining different structures allows workflow choice to reflect task
complexity and inference cost. A short synthesis task may benefit little
from a review loop that is useful for a difficult repair, so one
aggregate score can conceal which tasks benefit from which structures.
EvoAgentX provides a modular platform for generating, executing,
evaluating, and optimizing workflows, integrating TextGrad, AFlow, and
MIPRO to support changes to prompts, tool configurations, and topology
([Wang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib41)). Its scope shows why improvements to
a workflow system may involve several component types. FlowEvo makes the
interaction with assets explicit by compiling successful workflows into
executable skills, retaining them in a persistent bank, and retrieving
them for direct execution or later workflow construction ([Ren et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib154)). It also tracks downstream utility to suppress
skills associated with negative transfer. A discovered procedure can
thus move between $`w_{t}`$ and the skill state $`\mathcal{K}_{t}`$.
Retained skills expand the building blocks available to later workflow
search, while new workflows provide settings in which those skills are
exercised and reassessed. This creates a feedback loop between learning
reusable procedures and discovering how to organize them.

Selecting an existing branch exercises a workflow; retaining an
experience-derived revision constitutes an update. To examine a stage’s
contribution, let $`\mathcal{A}^{w}`$ use workflow $`w`$ and
$`w\setminus v`$ be a valid bypass of stage $`v`$, with the other agent
components fixed. Under matched evaluation conditions,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Gamma(v\mid w)=\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[s(\mathcal{A}^{w},q;B)-s(\mathcal{A}^{w\setminus v},q;B)\right].
``` |  | (25) |

This contribution depends on the surrounding workflow and bypass design.
A stage may help because it supplies evidence that another stage needs;
its effect cannot be inferred from its own output quality alone. A small
average contribution may also hide benefits on rare failures or
redundancy with another stage. The common budget $`B`$ constrains extra
computation, while recording actual cost and branch activation helps
explain how an evolved workflow achieves its result. The central
evaluation question is whether reorganizing execution makes useful
evidence influence decisions at the right time and at an acceptable
cost.

### 5.3 Multi-Agent Evolution

Multi-agent evolution concerns $`g_{t}`$, including the participating
agents, their responsibilities, and the mechanisms through which they
exchange and act on information. While a workflow describes dependencies
among stages, a team description also identifies who performs them and
how participants coordinate. A useful abstraction is

|     |                                                     |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       g_{t}=(V_{t}^{g},E_{t}^{g},\rho_{t}^{g},p_{t}^{g}),
       ```                                                  |     | (26) |

where $`V_{t}^{g}`$ is the participant set, $`E_{t}^{g}`$ contains
communication relations, $`\rho_{t}^{g}`$ assigns responsibilities, and
$`p_{t}^{g}`$ specifies interaction and decision rules. The latter
matters because the same communication graph can support different
handoff requirements, review responsibilities, or
disagreement-resolution procedures. For example, a reviewer may merely
suggest changes or require unresolved test failures to be addressed
before a patch is accepted. These arrangements give the same message
different consequences. Team evolution therefore concerns how
distributed evidence becomes a shared decision, including who can
challenge an assumption and who must act on the result.

Feedback-Driven Team Revision. EvoMAC obtains feedback from a testing
team and uses textual backpropagation to revise the coding team’s agent
instructions and connections ([Hu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib38)). These
updates are exercised in subsequent rounds of the same
software-development task. Meta-Team, introduced in *Evolve as a Team*,
preserves individual execution contexts and enables post-task discussion
to combine evidence distributed across participants ([Hao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib157)). It updates individual scaffolds, teammate
profiles, and team-level composition and rules, committing validated
changes to a reusable team scaffold. Their comparison highlights two
distinct reuse scopes, adaptation within a task and retained changes for
later tasks. They also expose a difficulty in assigning responsibility
for team failures. The last agent to produce an incorrect answer may
have acted on an incomplete handoff, while the relevant warning remained
in another participant’s context. For example, a tester may observe an
environment mismatch that a developer interprets as a code defect.
Improving the developer’s instructions alone may leave this failure
intact. Useful revision requires relating what each agent observed, what
it communicated, and how the recipient used that information. This can
reveal whether to improve an individual role, change a handoff, or
require explicit resolution of conflicting evidence.

Adaptive Topology and Mixed Update Targets. AgentConductor trains an
orchestrator to generate layered interaction graphs that reflect task
difficulty and communication cost ([Wang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib42)). At
inference, the orchestrator is frozen but can regenerate a topology
after execution feedback. Its persistent learning resides in the
orchestrator parameters, while its runtime effect is architectural
adaptation. SEMAG uses hierarchical planning, coding, debugging, and
discussion, together with an optional mechanism that selects updated
backbone models using retrieved information and sampled performance
([Peng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib37)). Its execution-dependent escalation
demonstrates adaptive coordination, although traversing predefined
stages alone does not establish a learned revision of coordination
rules. SAGE provides another boundary case. Its Challenger, Planner,
Solver, and Critic organize task generation, planning, solving, and
quality filtering, while verifier-based training updates their shared
model ([Peng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib156)). This supports collaborative
model improvement rather than independently demonstrating topology
evolution. Together, these cases distinguish the organization
instantiated for a task from the persistent mechanism that produces or
uses it. A different graph on the next task may reflect a learned
coordination policy or a fixed routing rule responding to different
inputs. Evaluation must identify which mechanism changed and whether its
choices remain useful beyond the situations that generated the update.
This distinction also connects architecture and model evolution without
treating every dynamically assembled team as a new learning event.

Collaboration during Evolution. GEA shares experience among a group of
candidate agents so that framework modifications and execution outcomes
from one lineage can inform others ([Weng et al., 2026](#bib.bib36)).
The resulting offspring retain their own revised implementations. Here,
the group organizes the improvement process and need not become a team
that jointly solves each downstream task. This distinction separates who
collaborates to produce an update from what the deployed update changes.
Sharing experience can broaden the evidence available to an offspring,
but a useful change in one lineage may rely on roles or interfaces
absent from another. The transferable unit therefore includes the
conditions under which an edit worked, as well as the edit itself.
Otherwise, combining successful local changes can introduce incompatible
assumptions.

Across these settings, evidence of team improvement should identify the
retained target and assess its contribution under the common execution
budget $`B`$. Additional participants can provide independent checks or
complementary evidence, but agreement can also arise from agents
repeating the same unsupported premise. Message count and consensus
alone therefore provide weak evidence of effective coordination.
Comparisons should account for total model calls, communication, and
latency, and examine whether revised roles or interaction rules change
which errors are detected and corrected. A positive $`\Delta J_{t}`$
establishes an overall gain under the specified conditions; attributing
that gain to coordination requires comparisons that separate these
revisions from added computation or simultaneous model and asset
updates.

## 6 Model Self-Evolution

Model self-evolution incorporates coding experience into the parameters
$`\theta_{t}`$ that shape subsequent agent decisions. Within
$`\mathcal{A}_{t}=(\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t},\theta_{t})`$, these
updates can change how the model localizes a defect, proposes a repair,
interprets feedback, or decides to verify its work. Parameter learning
can make an acquired behavior available across tasks without requiring
explicit retrieval of the originating experience. Its usefulness then
depends on whether the model preserves the conditions under which that
experience was informative. A successful repair can teach a transferable
strategy, but training on an incidental feature of the same repair may
produce an unreliable shortcut.

The following discussion distinguishes how training experience is
generated, how feedback becomes an optimization signal, and which model
role is updated. Self-play co-evolution changes the tasks or evaluators
that supply learning signals; environment-reward learning grounds
updates in task outcomes; harness co-evolution connects parameter
learning with changes to the surrounding execution system. These
mechanisms can overlap. We retain the earlier distinction between a
candidate update and its adoption, and use $`\Delta J_{t}`$ to assess
subsequent benefit. The formulas below describe shared mechanisms or
explicit comparison protocols; individual methods instantiate different
data, losses, and update schedules.

### 6.1 Self-Play Co-Evolution

Self-play makes the current system a source of its own future training
experience. An evolving model may generate tasks, solve them, construct
tests, or judge alternative outputs. Consequently, parameter updates
also change the distribution of experience available in the next round.
Let $`\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$ denote the training-task distribution. In a
batch of $`n_{t}`$ records, each $`(q_{i},\tau_{i},f_{i})`$ contains a
task, an execution trace, and its feedback. The records may include
several model roles and unsuccessful attempts. A common
data-construction abstraction is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{train}}=\operatorname{Curate}_{t}\!\left(\{(q_{i},\tau_{i},f_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n_{t}}\right).
``` |  | (27) |

Here $`q_{i}`$ is sampled from $`\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$, which may combine
generated and externally supplied tasks. Curation determines whether a
record supplies a demonstration, a preference, a reward, or privileged
information for a teacher. It can relabel or reweight experience as well
as reject it. The learning signal therefore depends on both what the
current system encounters and how those encounters are interpreted.

Task Generation and Curriculum. Self-Play SWE-RL uses a shared model for
bug injection and repair, combining consistency checks and
difficulty-sensitive rewards with joint reinforcement learning ([Wei et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib55)). Failed repairs can contribute further bug
states, connecting the solver’s current limitations to later training
tasks. Absolute Zero similarly trains a model to propose and solve
executable reasoning tasks, using execution to establish task outcomes
and solver success rates to guide task learnability ([Zhao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib159)). These mechanisms make task difficulty responsive to
the learner. However, difficulty alone does not establish relevance to
the intended deployment distribution. Anchored Self-Play addresses this
gap in code repair by mixing reference bugs into training and shaping
generated edits through similarity to reference changes ([Choi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib158)). This comparison separates three curriculum
requirements, whether tasks are valid, whether the model can learn from
them, and whether they exercise the capabilities needed later. Improving
one does not ensure the others. Analysis of learnable information gain
also links sustained self-play improvement to the information supplied
by the synthetic pipeline rather than data volume ([Liu et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib56)).

Coupled Code and Test Learning. ReVeal trains one policy for code
generation and self-verification, filtering generated tests against a
reference solution during training ([Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib69)).
CURE also uses a shared model in coder and tester roles, with reference
unit tests helping establish code quality and guide tester learning
([Wang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib70)). These reference signals anchor
different parts of the loop. A test that accepts a correct program need
not distinguish that program from plausible incorrect alternatives. For
a task $`q`$, let $`\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{-}(q)`$ be a nonempty set of
programs independently established as incorrect, and let $`v`$ be a test
checked against the task specification. Its empirical rejection rate is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{t}(v;q)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{-}(q)|}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{t}^{-}(q)}\mathbf{1}[\text{$v$ rejects $z$}].
``` |  | (28) |

This diagnostic separates test validity from its ability to expose known
errors. It does not measure coverage of unobserved failures. When no
independent labels are available, both program quality and test quality
must instead be inferred from their interactions, making mutual
agreement a less reliable anchor.

ZeroCoder studies this latter setting by estimating code and test
quality from execution consistency without reference code or tests in
its basic configuration ([Fan et al., 2026](#bib.bib71)). Its extensions
use a small labeled set for supervision and, for its dynamic Bayesian
selector, prior calibration. Sol-Ver trains solving and verification
through supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization ([Lin
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib72)). ACE uses a shared model as solver and
adversary, alternating solver fine-tuning with adversarial preference
learning ([Huang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib73)). Its generated inputs probe
runtime failures, while reference tests remain part of code selection.
The methods therefore differ in both the optimization procedure and the
claim supported by execution. Normal termination, agreement with
generated expectations, and agreement with reference tests are distinct
signals. A co-evolving evaluator is useful when it reveals weaknesses
that matter to the task; merely becoming more favorable toward the
co-evolving solver can conceal those weaknesses.

Learning from Privileged Experience. OPD-Evolver couples rapid memory
updates with slower parameter learning through on-policy
self-distillation ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib160)). The same evolver
supplies a teacher view conditioned on hindsight information and a
student view restricted to the information available when acting. Its
parameter updates cover selection, execution, memory writing, and
maintenance. Let $`x_{j}`$ be the student’s information at token
position $`j`$, including its own generated prefix, and let $`u_{j}`$
denote additional hindsight information. With frozen teacher parameters
$`\bar{\theta}_{t}`$, the token-level distillation loss has the form

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{distill}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x_{j},u_{j})\sim\mathcal{P}_{t}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\bar{\theta}_{t}}(\cdot\mid x_{j},u_{j})\,\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{j})\right).
``` |  | (29) |

Here $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ is formed from student rollouts and their
associated hindsight views; the teacher distribution receives no
gradient. Asset and architecture conditioning is implicit in the two
views. The teacher’s advantage comes from additional information,
without requiring a stronger external model. This is a boundary case
within self-play co-evolution, where the roles are informationally
asymmetric rather than adversarial. The update seeks to make lessons
from later outcomes useful at earlier decision points. The privileged
information must remain unavailable to the evaluated student if the
experiment is to establish that this capability was learned.

### 6.2 Environment-Reward RL

Environment-grounded learning derives supervision from what generated
programs or agent trajectories achieve. For a fixed training round,
write $`\mathcal{A}_{\theta}=(\mathcal{S}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t},\theta)`$
and let $`R_{t}(q,\tau)`$ be the scalar training return constructed from
execution feedback. An idealized policy objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{\theta}\;\mathbb{E}_{q\sim\mathcal{Q}_{t},\,\tau\sim\operatorname{Execute}(\mathcal{A}_{\theta},q,\mathcal{E}_{q})}[R_{t}(q,\tau)].
``` |  | (30) |

The trajectory notation denotes the trace component of execution, with
$`\mathcal{E}_{q}`$ the task environment. Holding assets and
architecture fixed isolates parameter optimization within the round.
Practical updates use finite samples and may include regularization. The
training return $`R_{t}`$ need not equal the evaluation score $`s`$, and
$`\mathcal{Q}_{t}`$ need not equal the held-out distribution
$`\mathcal{D}`$. These distinctions matter when a convenient reward
captures only part of the intended coding capability.

Guided Exploration and Credit Assignment. Agent-RLVR addresses sparse
success signals by having agents first attempt software tasks, then
reattempt failures with guidance derived from plans or environment
feedback ([Da et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)). Successful traces support an
initial supervised stage; successful and unsuccessful attempts supply
preferences for offline DPO. Guidance is used during training, while the
evaluated agent acts without it. For a common conditioning input $`x`$,
let $`y^{+}`$ and $`y^{-}`$ denote preferred and dispreferred
continuations in $`\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{pref}}`$. A
preference-learning objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\mathrm{pref}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^{+},y^{-})\sim\mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{pref}}}\log\operatorname{sigmoid}\!\left[\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{+}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{+}\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y^{-}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{-}\mid x)}\right].
``` |  | (31) |

Here $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ is a fixed reference policy and $`\beta>0`$
controls the preference scale. Execution determines the ordering; it
does not uniquely identify which intermediate decision caused the
outcome. A passing trace may contain redundant searches or incidental
edits. Pair construction and guidance therefore affect what the model
learns from the same terminal test result. Agent-RLVR’s reported
experiment covers one training cycle, so its gains should not be
interpreted as evidence of indefinitely repeated improvement.

Reward Semantics and Search Experience. SWE-RL uses issue descriptions,
code context, and reference patches from software history, rewarding
similarity between generated and reference patches with a penalty for
invalid formatting ([Wei et al., 2025b](#bib.bib50)). It optimizes the
model with GRPO. Its supervision is grounded in software evolution data,
but the training reward is not a unit-test execution verdict. Similarity
can provide an inexpensive signal while favoring the particular
implementation represented by the reference patch. The method therefore
illustrates why software provenance, executable verification, and
autonomous task generation must be distinguished when comparing learning
loops.

SOAR supplies a complementary boundary case under this feedback-based
category ([Pourcel et al., 2025](#bib.bib161)). It alternates
evolutionary program search with supervised learning from the resulting
attempts, improving both program sampling and refinement. Hindsight
relabeling converts an unsuccessful program into a solution for a
different task consistent with its actual outputs. Thus, execution
feedback can support parameter learning without serving as a direct
policy-gradient reward. Relabeling preserves useful computation from
failed search, but changes what the resulting training pair teaches. A
program that failed the original specification is not thereby a
successful solution to that specification. SOAR’s inclusion highlights a
shared feedback source across different optimization mechanisms.

Feedback Infrastructure and Transfer. SWE-Gym and R2E-Gym provide
executable environments and training pipelines for agents and verifiers
([Pan et al., 2025](#bib.bib51), [Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib53));
SWE-RM learns execution-free feedback for candidate selection and policy
improvement ([Shum et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)). Their contribution
includes making informative experience or scalable evaluation available
to a learning loop. The resulting model gains still depend on how that
feedback is used. Learned rewards can reduce execution cost, but policy
optimization may exploit their errors; executable tests provide concrete
evidence, but cover only specified cases. Evaluation should therefore
retain independent outcome checks and compare updated policies under the
same budget $`B`$. Training and data-collection costs should be reported
separately, especially when guidance or repeated search makes successful
traces expensive.

### 6.3 Harness Co-Evolution

The harness $`h_{t}`$ shapes both the model’s current execution and the
experience available for its next update. Changing action interfaces,
feedback delivery, or recovery rules can make different trajectories
reachable. Conversely, parameter learning can change which interventions
remain useful. Harness co-evolution therefore concerns this feedback
between learned behavior and execution control. It also distinguishes
learning to solve tasks from learning to modify the system that solves
them.

Learning the Editing Policy. Harness-R1 trains a dedicated harness
engineer through supervised initialization and online GRPO, while
freezing the target agent during engineer training ([Shao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib105)). Failure traces condition executable patches, and
rerunning the target with a patch supplies the engineer’s reward. To
describe this separation, let $`\omega`$ denote editor parameters,
$`b_{t}`$ the failure evidence, and $`\mathcal{A}_{t}^{e}`$ the target
with edit $`e`$ installed. For an installable edit evaluated on a
nonempty matched task batch $`\mathcal{V}_{t}`$, the empirical utility
change can be written as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{\Delta}_{t}(e)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{t}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}_{t}}[s(\mathcal{A}_{t}^{e},q;B)-s(\mathcal{A}_{t},q;B)].
``` |  | (32) |

The batch includes previously successful cases so that regressions
contribute to the signal. Define $`r_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}}(e)`$ to equal
this change for a completed valid evaluation and zero for invalid or
incomplete candidates. The corresponding editor objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\max_{\omega}\;\mathbb{E}_{e\sim\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid b_{t})}[r_{t}^{\mathrm{edit}}(e)].
``` |  | (33) |

The expectation also includes the training distribution of failure
bundles. The updated parameters belong to the editor, while the target
receives an architectural intervention. Harness-R1 evaluates this
mechanism on WebShop, ALFWorld, and DBBench; its evidence concerns
executable harness engineering across interactive domains, rather than a
direct repository-repair benchmark. The learned capability is to produce
useful edits from new failures, so transfer of the editor must be
distinguished from reuse of one particular patch.

From Harness Search to Model Learning. HELIX proposes a
build–update–rebuild process in which harness variants produce verified
experience for model updating, followed by harness rebuilding for the
changed model ([Fan and Huang, 2026](#bib.bib93)). It retains
source-traceable execution records for related candidates, including
successful repairs, regressions, and near misses, and materializes
supervised, critic, filtering, and preference data. Such contrasts can
preserve why two executions differed, instead of retaining only the best
final patch. Its reported study demonstrates harness search and
training-data construction, but does not train an updated model. It
therefore supports the handoff from architecture evolution to parameter
learning, while leaving the complete repeated cycle to be evaluated.

To assess a completed coupled update, the old and new model–harness
combinations should be compared under matched conditions. For
$`a,b\in\{0,1\}`$, let $`j_{ab}`$ be the expected score under
$`\mathcal{D}`$ and budget $`B`$ when model parameters $`\theta_{t+a}`$
are paired with harness $`h_{t+b}`$. All four combinations must have
compatible interfaces. Assets, workflow, and team organization are held
fixed for this comparison. The interaction contrast is

|     |                                               |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       I_{t}^{\theta,h}=j_{11}-j_{10}-j_{01}+j_{00}.
       ```                                            |     | (34) |

A positive value means the combined change exceeds the sum of the
isolated changes on the chosen score scale; it does not by itself imply
positive total improvement, which requires $`j_{11}>j_{00}`$. The
contrast is specific to the tested configurations, distribution, and
budget. It makes a central question of co-evolution explicit, whether
parameter learning and harness revision reinforce one another or merely
contribute separate gains. Across all three model-evolution mechanisms,
stronger training signals matter only when their effects survive
adoption and improve coding behavior.

## 7 Coding Feedback and Evolution Dynamics

Coding environments expose unusually rich evidence about the
consequences of agent actions. A single attempt can leave a patch, build
status, test verdicts, an exception stack, a sequence of tool calls,
resource measurements, and a developer correction. These observations
make software engineering a natural setting for self-evolution because
they can often be attached to inspectable artifacts and reproduced in an
executable environment. Their precision does not remove the central
difficulty. A test may establish that one patch satisfies one checked
property while providing insufficient support for a memory, skill, or
harness rule that will influence many later tasks. We therefore organize
the discussion around four questions: why coding environments provide
distinctive signals, what each signal reveals, how methods convert
signals into persistent updates, and when those updates are made.

### 7.1 Why Coding Is a Natural Domain for Self-Evolution

Coding has played a formative role in agent research and has been one of
the earliest and most sustained application frontiers for LLM-based
agents. It supplies an instrumented environment, not only a task domain,
in which a model can execute an action, observe its consequences, and
revise its behavior. Codex and AlphaCode established execution-based
evaluation early in the development of language models for code ([Chen
et al., 2021](#bib.bib57), [Li et al., 2022](#bib.bib61)).
Repository-level systems then extended this generate–execute–inspect
loop to file navigation, command-line tools, testing, and multi-step
repair ([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib6), [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib7), [Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib8)). Tool-mediated
action, environment feedback, and verifier-guided revision were
consequently developed or stress-tested early in coding settings. These
patterns now reach other domains, where code serves as an operational
medium for action, state, and verification ([Ning and others,
2026](#bib.bib32)). Coding is therefore a mature proving ground for
agents, with both attempted changes and much of their evidence already
represented in machine-readable form.

A coding task is embedded in a repository snapshot, dependency
configuration, toolchain, and execution environment. One attempt can
leave a patch, build status, named test failures, an exception stack,
tool-call history, resource measurements, and review comments. We
represent the evidence associated with one coding event as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{F}_{t}=(y_{t},d_{t},\tau_{t},r_{t},q_{t},h_{t},m_{t};e_{t},p_{t}),
``` |  | (35) |

where $`y_{t}`$ records execution outcomes, $`d_{t}`$ diagnostic
evidence, $`\tau_{t}`$ the coding trajectory, $`r_{t}`$ repository
context, $`q_{t}`$ software-quality attributes, $`h_{t}`$ human
judgments, and $`m_{t}`$ model judgments. The environment state
$`e_{t}`$ and provenance $`p_{t}`$ bind those observations to a
repository revision, dependency state, tool version, candidate change,
and evaluator. This structure matters because an identical patch can
produce a different result after a dependency update, and the same score
has a different meaning when it comes from a regression suite, a model
judge, or a developer review.

Three properties distinguish these signals as a basis for evolution.

- •
  Specificity. Coding feedback often identifies a concrete violated
  condition. A compiler can report an error class and source location, a
  unit test can name the failed assertion and expose expected and
  observed behavior, and a static analyzer can identify a rule and code
  region. The signal can therefore constrain both *what* should change
  and *where* the agent should look. Executable benchmarks and training
  environments exploit this property to turn test outcomes into
  validation or learning signals ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib57), [Pan
  et al., 2025](#bib.bib51), [Da et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)). Specificity
  is nevertheless local to the checked property. A passing suite is a
  partial oracle, and converting one failure into a general memory,
  skill, or harness rule still requires identifying the conditions under
  which that lesson applies.
- •
  Traceability. Software work leaves a causal record that can be
  inspected after execution. Issues state the requested behavior,
  version control identifies the repository state, diffs record the
  proposed intervention, and trajectories connect searches, edits,
  commands, and responses. SWE-bench grounds evaluation in
  issue–repository–patch relations, while SWE-agent shows how an
  agent–computer interface makes repository actions and their feedback
  explicit ([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib6), [Yang et al.,
  2024](#bib.bib7)). This lineage lets an evolution mechanism attach
  provenance to a retained update and assign credit more precisely than
  a final reward alone. It also exposes confounders. A successful patch
  may follow several irrelevant actions, whereas a failed attempt may
  contain a correct diagnosis followed by an incorrect edit.
- •
  Reproducibility. A repository revision, environment image, command,
  and test suite can define a replayable experiment. The same candidate
  can be executed again, compared with its parent under matched
  conditions, and checked for regressions before adoption. SWE-Gym and
  R2E-Gym package coding tasks as executable environments, and
  SWE-bench-Live provides task-specific container images and repeated
  validation to improve reproducibility ([Pan et al., 2025](#bib.bib51),
  [Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib53), [Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib170)).
  Reproducibility here is conditional rather than absolute. Flaky tests,
  external services, dependency drift, hardware, and stochastic agent
  decisions can still change an outcome. Coding environments are
  distinctive because these conditions can often be recorded, replayed,
  and tested for instability.

Together, specificity, traceability, and reproducibility shorten the
path from an observed failure to an addressable and testable candidate
update. Other agent environments may provide one or two of these
properties, but software engineering routinely combines all three
through executable artifacts, version history, and automated checks.
This combination explains why coding has been an important proving
ground for self-correction and agent evolution. It does not, however,
collapse task verification into evolution evaluation. Tests directly
judge the current software artifact; only retained reuse and matched
evaluation on later cases can show that the changed agent has improved.

### 7.2 What Coding Signals Reveal

The properties established above explain why software evidence is
useful, but an evolution mechanism still depends on which evidence it
actually consumes. We distinguish seven non-exclusive signal classes
throughout this survey: execution outcomes (E), diagnostic evidence (D),
coding trajectories (T), repository context (R), quality attributes (Q),
human judgments (H), and model judgments (M). The first five classes are
grounded in software execution, process, state, or properties. H and M
instead record evaluative judgments: H reflects developer or
organizational assessment, whereas M reflects a learned evaluator whose
reliability depends on both the evaluator and its input evidence. The
codes describe evidence used to construct, revise, or select a
persistent update. They do not describe the benchmark on which the
resulting agent is later evaluated. A method may receive several codes
because one coding event can expose several views of the same outcome.
For example, a failed integration test supplies an execution outcome
(E), its stack trace supplies diagnostic evidence (D), the preceding
tool calls form a trajectory (T), and the repository revision defines
the conditions under which the evidence is valid (R).

|  Signal class |  Observable evidence |  Question answered |  Evolutionary role and validity boundary |
|----|----|----|----|
|  E Execution outcomes |  Unit and integration tests, builds, executions, patch verifiers |  Did the artifact satisfy an executable check? |  Validate or select candidates within observed test coverage. |
|  D Diagnostic evidence |  Compiler messages, test logs, exceptions, build and tool failures |  Where and how did the failure appear? |  Locate update targets; symptoms may not identify their causes. |
|  T Coding trajectories |  Searches, inspections, edits, tests, retries, and recovery actions |  How was the result produced? |  Extract procedures; final success provides incomplete credit. |
|  R Repository context |  Issues, commits, pull requests, diffs, interfaces, dependencies, revisions |  When is reuse valid? |  Ground retrieval and reuse despite repository and dependency drift. |
|  Q Quality attributes |  Efficiency, security, maintainability, and vulnerability repair |  Which quality attributes improved? |  Assess non-functional gains and competing objectives. |
|  H Human judgments |  Code review, edits, acceptance, rejection, corrections, preferences |  What do developers or organizations value? |  Convey intent and authority under sparse, subjective review. |
|  M Model judgments |  LLM critiques, rankings, credit assignments, learned rewards |  How does an evaluator assess the evidence? |  Scale semantic evaluation, subject to evaluator reliability. |

Table 4: Seven non-exclusive signal classes used by coding-agent
evolution mechanisms. The codes identify evidence consumed during
updating rather than the benchmark used for final evaluation.

Execution Outcomes (E). Execution outcomes record whether a software
artifact satisfies an operational condition. They include unit and
integration tests, compilation, interpretation, patch verifiers,
task-resolution checks, and measured execution outcomes. DGM, Mendel GM,
and Huxley GM use verified coding performance to select agent variants
across generations, while SICA retains source-level self-modifications
according to coding-task results ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib18),
[Anonymous, 2026](#bib.bib47), [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib48),
[Robeyns et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)). AFlow uses execution outcomes to
select workflows, and Agent-RLVR turns unit-test results into rewards
for policy learning ([Zhang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib40), [Da et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52)). The same class of evidence can therefore drive
architecture or model evolution. Its strength is an explicit and
repeatable verdict; its boundary is the property checked. Compilation
confirms acceptance by a build process, and a passing test confirms only
the encoded assertions. Infrastructure failure, test non-execution, and
a completed negative verdict must also remain distinguishable because
they support different updates.

Diagnostic Evidence (D). Diagnostic evidence describes where and how
execution failed. It includes compiler messages, assertion output,
exception stacks, test logs, shell output, dependency conflicts, build
failures, and tool errors. Live-SWE-agent uses command and test feedback
while revising utilities, whereas HarnessFix and HELIX use failed
trajectories and diagnostic traces to identify editable harness
components ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib19), [Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib75), [Fan and Huang, 2026](#bib.bib93)). ReVeal, CURE,
ZeroCoder, and Sol-Ver similarly use interpreter feedback, generated
tests, or execution failures to improve coder–verifier behavior ([Jin et
al., 2025](#bib.bib69), [Wang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib70), [Fan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib71), [Lin et al., 2025b](#bib.bib72)). Diagnostics give
failure an address, making them especially useful for deciding what to
revise. That address may still identify a symptom. An exception in a
caller may originate in an earlier interface change, while an import
error may reflect the environment rather than the application code.

Coding Trajectories (T). A coding trajectory records how an attempt
unfolds through repository search, fault localization, file inspection,
editing, testing, failed branches, retries, and recovery. Its value lies
in retaining process information discarded by a final score. SAGE
compresses search–edit–test rollouts into reusable plans; SWE-Exp,
EvoCoder, and Subtask Memory transform issue-resolution histories into
experience at episode, repository, or subtask granularity ([Hayashi et
al., 2025](#bib.bib65), [Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20), [Lin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib66), [Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib68)). CODESKILL and
Socratic-SWE further distill traces into skills for future tasks ([Li et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib43), [Xiao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib45)). Trajectories
support procedural abstraction and credit assignment, but they do not
solve either problem automatically. Successful traces can contain
ineffective actions, and failed traces can contain a correct diagnosis
followed by a faulty edit. Labeling every step with the final outcome
would preserve both kinds of error.

Repository Context (R). Repository context describes the persistent
software setting in which an experience was produced. They include
issues, commits, pull requests, changed files, directory structure,
interfaces, cross-file dependencies, line-level relevance, and
repository revisions. Repository Memory links commit history, issues,
and file changes to later localization, while GSkill and GSE use
repository structure, conventions, and interaction histories when
forming reusable capabilities ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21), [Tan et
al., 2026](#bib.bib44), [Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib89)). SWE-Pruner
learns which code should remain visible, and Libra revises repository
catalogs after localization failures ([Wang et al., 2026i](#bib.bib95),
[Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)). These signals do more than supply
context. They define applicability. A workaround tied to one dependency
version should not become an unconditional rule, and an accepted
historical patch is evidence about one development state rather than the
only valid implementation.

Quality Attributes (Q). Quality attributes describe software properties
beyond functional correctness, including runtime, memory use, resource
consumption, security, vulnerability removal, maintainability, and
reviewability. EffiSkill derives optimization skills from slow-to-fast
program pairs and measured efficiency gains, while EvoRepair combines
repair outcomes with vulnerability patterns to retain security-repair
experience ([Wang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib67), [Hu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)). Such signals are essential when two patches both
pass tests but differ in operational or engineering value. They also
introduce multi-objective trade-offs. An update that improves latency
can increase memory use, and a security hardening rule can reduce
compatibility. The metric, workload, and acceptable trade-off must
therefore remain attached to the retained update.

Human Judgments (H). Human judgments arise from ordinary software
collaboration. They include code-review comments, developer edits,
acceptance or rejection, corrections, project conventions, and personal
preferences. Behavioral Rules turns accepted review comments into
persistent instructions and tracks whether the corresponding errors
recur. Personalized Skills extracts user-specific procedures from
developer–agent histories, and Ouroboros incorporates reviewed commits
and feedback about weaknesses in the coding-agent core ([Aggarwal and
Ghalaty, 2026](#bib.bib91), [Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib92),
[Razzhigaev et al., 2026](#bib.bib106)). Human judgments can express
intent, maintainability, and organizational authority that tests omit.
It is also sparse, costly, and sometimes subjective, so the identity and
scope of the feedback provider matter when deciding whether a preference
should become a general rule.

Model Judgments (M). Model judgments are produced by an LLM judge,
critic, reward model, or peer agent rather than directly by program
execution or a developer. It includes natural-language diagnoses,
candidate rankings, patch scores, responsibility assignments, and
learned reward estimates. JUDGEFLOW uses a judge to rank the
responsibility of workflow blocks, SIFT screens candidate harness
patches before expensive execution, and SWE-RM predicts the quality of
software-engineering trajectories ([Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib155), [Fu
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib63), [Shum et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)). M makes
dense and scalable feedback available when execution is expensive or
when a judgment requires semantic interpretation. Its output is
nevertheless an inference, not an independent software fact. A confident
critique may mislocalize a failure, and a reward model may preserve
biases in its training comparisons. When a model judge consumes tests,
diagnostics, trajectories, or repository evidence, we assign M together
with the corresponding E, D, T, or R codes; an ungrounded model score
receives M alone.

The seven codes are non-exclusive evidence labels rather than a ranking
of reliability. Execution outcomes are usually precise but narrow;
trajectories and human judgments are semantically richer but require
interpretation; model judgments are scalable but inherit the coverage,
provenance, and failure modes of both its inputs and evaluator. A method
evaluated on a coding benchmark does not automatically receive a
coding-specific evidence code. The label records what the evolution loop
actually consumes while constructing or selecting its update.

We manually annotated all 108 methods in Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Taxonomy of Self-Evolving Coding Agents ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
under this criterion. Execution outcomes dominate (E, 99), followed by
trajectories (T, 87), diagnostics (D, 55), model judgments (M, 43),
repository context (R, 37), quality attributes (Q, 21), and human
judgments (H, 5).

The distribution exposes a sharp grounding imbalance. Current systems
learn mainly from what software can execute and what agent runtimes can
record, while developer intent remains weakly represented. Grouping the
same annotations by persistent update target shows that this imbalance
is structured rather than uniform. Memory methods rely most heavily on
trajectories and repository context, consistent with retaining an
experience together with the conditions under which it remains
applicable. Skill and tool methods draw on the broadest mix of signals
and use quality attributes more often than other targets, because a
reusable operation must be judged by more than task completion alone.
Harness evolution has the highest reliance on model judgments, which
help assign responsibility among interacting runtime components before
executable checks validate a proposed repair. Model evolution,
meanwhile, uses execution outcomes and trajectories in every surveyed
method and diagnostics in most of them. Signal choice is therefore
coupled to what evolves. Each update target observes a different slice
of software development and inherits the blind spots of that evidence.

### 7.3 How Signals Drive Agent Evolution

A failed test is evidence, not yet an agent update. Its diagnosis can be
stored as memory, abstracted into a debugging skill, used to revise a
validation workflow, or converted into training supervision. The same
software event can therefore produce changes with different reach and
failure modes.

The conversion mechanism determines which part of the evidence becomes a
lesson and how it can affect future work. We therefore examine
experience generation, candidate construction, and selection for reuse.
Self-play generates new tasks and trajectories; supervised fine-tuning
(SFT), preference optimization, and reinforcement learning (RL) fit
model parameters to such records; program search compares executable
agent structures. These operations can be combined. Signal type and
retained component alone do not reveal how an agent evolves.

Constructing experience. Many methods begin with trajectories from
actual coding attempts, including failed edits and their diagnostics.
SWE-Exp distills both successful and failed repairs, while Agent-RLVR
uses unit-test results to identify failed attempts and then obtains
guided reattempts that provide otherwise scarce successful trajectories
([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20), [Da et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)).
Self-Play SWE-RL (SSR) takes a different route: a shared agent injects
bugs into sandboxed repositories, specifies them through test patches,
and attempts to repair them. The generated cases change with the agent’s
capabilities and supply experience for joint RL ([Wei et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib55)). Thus, self-play is a way to construct a training
distribution, not itself an update to the deployed agent. Generated
tasks must still be valid, informative, and relevant to later coding
work.

Distilling reusable behavior. Non-parametric methods select or
synthesize something that can be used again without retraining the task
model. SWE-Exp compresses a repair attempt into issue-resolution
experience; Repository Memory and Agent KB organize repository facts and
past interactions for later retrieval ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20),
[Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21), [Tang et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)).
Retrieval is part of the mechanism: an accurate lesson that is never
surfaced, or is applied to a different repository state, cannot improve
the next decision. CODESKILL instead extracts procedures at several
granularities and maintains a compact skill bank. It trains the
skill-management policy with RL using both rubric feedback and
verifiable outcomes from a frozen downstream coding agent ([Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib43)). This is an important cross-layer case: RL optimizes
the manager, while the reusable resource presented to the coding agent
is a skill. Socratic-SWE uses trace-derived skills to help construct
training tasks, and Live-SWE-agent writes and revises callable utilities
during issue resolution ([Xiao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib45), [Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)). Skill abstraction and tool synthesis increase reuse,
but can omit the conditions under which the original repair worked.

Searching executable structures. Other methods make the agent
implementation itself a candidate. HarnessFix turns recurring failure
diagnoses into scoped harness repairs, while EvoMAC uses testing-team
feedback to revise coding-team instructions and connections ([Chen et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib75), [Hu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib38)). DGM samples an
agent from an archive, uses a foundation model to modify its source
code, evaluates the variant on coding tasks, and keeps alternative
lineages available for later search ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib18)).
AFlow represents workflows as code and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search,
code edits, and execution feedback to explore their structure ([Zhang et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib40)). In these systems, feedback guides proposal or
selection; it does not specify the correct architecture. The measured
result depends on both the selected implementation and the search budget
used to discover it.

Optimizing model parameters. When the retained change is a model, the
training record and optimization rule must be stated separately.
Agent-RLVR uses successful initial trajectories for SFT, then guided
retries of failures to construct successful–unsuccessful pairs for
offline DPO ([Da et al., 2025](#bib.bib52)). SWE-RL instead trains on
historical issue and patch pairs using GRPO; its inexpensive reward
measures similarity to the reference patch, rather than unit-test
success ([Wei et al., 2025b](#bib.bib50)). Self-Play SWE-RL uses
generated bug-repair episodes for joint RL ([Wei et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib55)). These methods all learn from software-related
evidence, but they optimize against different targets. A test verdict,
reference-patch similarity, and a preference pair can rank the same
trajectory differently. Parameter learning can spread such judgments
across many future decisions, making reward design and data curation as
consequential as the optimizer.

Table

Signal conversion can amplify errors. Self-authored verification can
confidently approve invalid updates; external audits improve reliability
([Guo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib187)). Memory Reward Inflation shows failed
episodes being overrated and retrieved; correction raises BIRD execution
accuracy from 54.0% to 56.9% ([Asadolahi et al., 2026](#bib.bib188)).
Phantom Guardrails reports nonexistent failures inducing persistent
harness rules in 15 of 60 runs ([Wang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib189)).
These cases show why adoption requires independent checks of provenance
and applicability.

### 7.4 When to Evolve

The time at which feedback appears need not be the time at which the
agent changes. Four events should be distinguished:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
t_{\mathrm{observe}}\leq t_{\mathrm{propose}}\leq t_{\mathrm{adopt}}\leq t_{\mathrm{reuse}}.
``` |  | (36) |

An agent may observe a compiler error immediately, propose a tool after
several failed commands, adopt it only after validation, and reuse it
later in the same task or in a future repository. Online feedback
therefore does not by itself establish online evolution. Timing is
defined by when a persistent change enters later execution.

Within-Task Evolution. Within-task evolution adopts an update before the
current task ends, shortening the distance between feedback and
behavioral change. Live-SWE-agent creates and revises utilities while
resolving an issue, and EvoMAC updates coding-team instructions and
connections across rounds of the same development task ([Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19), [Hu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib38)). This timing can
exploit task-local state and test a candidate quickly, but the available
evidence is incomplete and highly correlated with the current
trajectory. A provisional update is appropriate when its scope is narrow
and its effects can be reversed.

Post-Task Evolution. Post-task evolution forms and adopts an update
after one task has finished. It can use the complete trajectory, final
validation results, and regressions that were unavailable at the first
failure. SWE-Exp distills finished attempts, CODESKILL constructs and
maintains skills from accumulated coding activity, and HarnessFix turns
recurring failed trajectories into scoped harness repairs ([Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib20), [Li et al., 2026c](#bib.bib43), [Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib75)). Waiting improves the evidence available for credit
assignment, although it delays reuse and may discard transient state
needed to understand the failure.

Cross-Task Evolution. Cross-task evolution aggregates evidence from
multiple tasks or evolution stages before committing broader changes.
DGM evaluates generations of agent implementations, AFlow searches
workflows over repeated benchmark executions, and Agent-RLVR collects
guided trajectories before parameter optimization ([Zhang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib18), [Zhang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib40), [Da et al.,
2025](#bib.bib52)). Accumulation can reveal recurring patterns and
support stronger validation, making it suitable for architecture and
model updates with a wider blast radius. It also increases adaptation
latency and the opportunity to fit the tasks used for proposal and
selection.

The timing choice therefore trades responsiveness against evidential
breadth. Local asset updates can often be attempted early because they
are scoped and reversible. Architecture changes usually require broader
regression evidence, while parameter updates commonly aggregate many
trajectories before training. This is a tendency rather than a fixed
correspondence. The appropriate time is determined by the uncertainty of
$`\mathcal{F}_{t}`$, the intervention depth of $`\widehat{u}_{t}`$, its
reuse scope $`\rho_{t}`$, and the cost of reversing it. Across all
timings, the evolution claim begins when a candidate is adopted into
later execution, and the improvement claim still requires a positive
effect under the evaluation scope and budget developed next.

## 8 Benchmarks and Evaluation

Evaluating a self-evolving coding agent involves two coupled objects:
the software artifact produced for the current task and the persistent
agent state that shapes subsequent tasks. Tests, compilers, and
reviewers can assess the artifact directly, but they supervise the
retained update only indirectly. Let $`p_{t}`$ denote a patch and
$`V(p_{t};e_{t})`$ its validation result in environment $`e_{t}`$. Even
a successful validation does not establish a beneficial agent update,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(p_{t};e_{t})=1\quad\text{does not establish}\quad\Delta J_{t}>0.
``` |  | (37) |

A valid patch can yield an overgeneralized memory, an unnecessary skill,
or a harness rule that harms later tasks. Conversely, an unsuccessful
attempt can contain a correct diagnosis that becomes useful after its
conditions are identified. Evaluation must therefore distinguish
artifact correctness from the behavioral contribution of the update
derived from that artifact.

Coding benchmarks further play three roles in an evolution pipeline.
Their tasks and signals may construct updates, select which candidate
updates are retained, or report the final performance of the evolved
agent. Reusing the same evidence across these roles can make repeated
adaptation to the evaluator look like general improvement. A benchmark
specifies where the agent acts and how task outcomes are checked; it
does not by itself define a valid evaluation of evolution. The protocol
must additionally specify what persists, which evidence influences
adoption, what budget is available, and how far the claimed reuse
extends.
````
