````math
### 8.1 Conventional Coding Benchmarks Used for Evolution

Most self-evolving coding agents are evaluated in benchmarks originally
designed to measure coding competence rather than change in the agent
itself. These benchmarks remain valuable because they provide executable
tasks, observable trajectories, and software-specific outcome checks.
Their role in an evolution study, however, depends on both the coding
behavior they expose and the claims their evaluation unit can support.
We group the commonly used settings into repository-level issue
resolution, function-level and competition-style programming, and
operational or specialized software tasks. Table
[6](#S8.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 8 Benchmarks and Evaluation ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
lists representative datasets in these three groups and provides links
to their available resources.

Repository-level issue resolution. Repository-level benchmarks expose
issues, source trees, dependency states, execution traces, patches, and
regression outcomes. SWE-bench introduced this setting using real GitHub
issues and corresponding pull requests, while SWE-bench Lite, SWE-bench
Verified, and SWE-Bench Pro refine task quality, validation, and
difficulty ([Jimenez et al., 2023](#bib.bib6), [Deng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)). SWE-Gym further turns repository tasks into
executable environments for agent training and evaluation ([Pan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib51)). These settings expose realistic evidence for
constructing updates because an experience can be grounded in a
repository revision and its patch can be checked against later software
behavior. In their usual episodic use, however, the evaluation unit
remains an issue–patch pair. The resulting score shows whether the
current agent solves sampled issues, not whether an update produced from
issue $`c_{i}`$ improves the agent on a later issue $`c_{j}`$.

Function-level and competition-style programming. HumanEval and MBPP
provide concise specifications and executable tests, while APPS,
CodeContests, and LiveCodeBench extend the difficulty and diversity of
programming problems ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib57), [Austin et al.,
2021](#bib.bib58), [Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib59), [Li et al.,
2022](#bib.bib61), [Jain et al., 2024](#bib.bib60)). Their controlled
interfaces make them useful for comparing model learning and workflow
search, including systems such as SEMAG and SEW ([Peng et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib37), [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). They reveal whether
an update improves program synthesis under a stable oracle, but usually
provide little evidence about repository navigation or dependency
management. Repeated attempts can expose self-correction and algorithmic
refinement within a problem, but a reset between problems removes the
persistence needed to test whether the agent carries an improvement
forward.

Operational and specialized software settings. Terminal-Bench evaluates
long-horizon interaction with terminals and execution harnesses
([Merrill et al., 2026](#bib.bib62)). Repository understanding,
compilation, and environment construction are examined through
LongCodeQA, CompileBench, Repo2Run, EnvBench, and EnConda-Bench ([Wang
et al., 2026i](#bib.bib95), [Ren et al., 2026a](#bib.bib84), [Guo et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib96)). Security and efficiency benchmarks add
objectives not captured by functional tests. PATCHEVAL, SEC-bench, and
VUL4J examine vulnerability repair, while PIE and Mercury measure
program optimization ([Hu et al., 2026](#bib.bib22), [Wang et al.,
2026j](#bib.bib67)). Finally, developer-agent sessions expose review,
acceptance, and repeated use in real projects ([Aggarwal and Ghalaty,
2026](#bib.bib91), [Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib92)). Together, these
settings broaden the observable consequences of evolution. They also
make comparisons harder because environment state, workloads, tool
versions, and human assistance can change along with the agent. Their
value is therefore greatest when the relevant state can be replayed and
competing agents receive matched opportunities to act.

These conventional benchmarks provide the environments and feedback from
which an agent may evolve, but they do not by themselves identify
evolution. This limitation becomes critical when the same tasks or test
signals generate trajectories, guide candidate selection, and report
final performance. Repeated adaptation can then raise the score without
producing a reusable improvement. Static task collections also face
solution leakage, weak tests, and training contamination, motivating
filtered and continuously refreshed variants ([Aleithan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib168), [Badertdinov et al., 2025](#bib.bib169), [Zhang et
al., 2025d](#bib.bib170)). These concerns affect coding-agent evaluation
broadly; the additional challenge for self-evolution is to show that a
retained change, rather than repeated exposure to the evaluator, causes
better future behavior.

### 8.2 Benchmarks Designed to Evaluate Evolution

Evolution-oriented benchmarks differ in the object whose change they
evaluate, rather than in when an update occurs. We distinguish changes
to a task solution, a software artifact, and persistent agent state.
Evidence at one level does not establish change at the next.

Solution-Level Adaptation. EvoCodeBench tracks correctness, runtime,
memory use, and algorithmic efficiency across successive refinements of
one solution ([Zhang et al., 2026g](#bib.bib171)). It tests whether
feedback improves the current solution. If the agent is reset before the
next problem, the result does not show that the state used for future
tasks has changed.

Artifact-Level Evolution. SWE-EVO uses release-scale tasks that require
coordinated changes across files while preserving existing behavior
([Thai et al., 2025](#bib.bib172)). It measures sustained change to a
software artifact, but a repository can evolve while its agent remains
fixed. The result supports agent evolution only when earlier experience
is retained in $`S_{t}`$, $`H_{t}`$, or $`\theta_{t}`$ and affects later
decisions.

Persistent Agent-State Evolution. These benchmarks carry agent state
across tasks or fresh sessions. LifelongAgentBench tests accumulation
and transfer over interdependent task sequences ([Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib173)). SkillFlow evaluates skill discovery, repair, reuse,
and regression, while SkillLearnBench connects skill quality and
invocation to task outcomes ([Zhang et al., 2026m](#bib.bib174), [Zhong
et al., 2026](#bib.bib177)). PAST-Bench compares matched persistence-on
and persistence-off conditions, and SEA-Eval jointly tracks reliability,
long-term performance, and token use over sequential streams ([Xue et
al., 2026](#bib.bib175), [Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib176)). MemoryArena
and Evo-Memory isolate memory accumulation, revision, and behavioral
reuse ([He et al., 2026](#bib.bib179), [Wei et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib180)). Together, these protocols test whether retained
experience changes later behavior; equal success rates may still conceal
different trajectories and costs.

Causal Attribution Protocols. An evolution benchmark must combine
realistic software tasks with sequential state and attribution controls.
It should separate the cases used to construct updates, select
candidates, and report final performance. Let
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{upd}}`$, $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{sel}}`$, and
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{eval}}`$ denote these roles. Because candidate
selection is part of improvement, final evaluation must remain insulated
from both update construction and selection. Repository, temporal, and
defect-family separation is stronger than a random issue split when
cases can share files, APIs, tests, or solution patterns.

GDPevo illustrates this principle by distributing atomic rules across
update tasks and recombining them in held-out cases ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib178)). Its business workflows are not coding tasks, but
the same design can test new combinations of APIs, defect families,
repository structures, or validation requirements.

Attribution further requires a matched frozen agent that receives the
same observations, tools, budget, and repair opportunities but does not
retain the candidate update. Component hybrids such as
$`(S_{t+1},H_{t},\theta_{t})`$, $`(S_{t},H_{t+1},\theta_{t})`$, and
$`(S_{t},H_{t},\theta_{t+1})`$ can locate the source of a gain when
components are exchangeable. Checkpoints, repeated evaluation of earlier
groups, and multiple task orders then reveal retention, forgetting, and
curriculum effects. These controls turn a coding benchmark into an
experiment about a changing agent.

### 8.3 Measuring Benefit, Regression, and Cost

Pass rate, resolve rate, repair rate, benchmark score, and Pass@$`k`$
remain necessary measures of software outcomes ([Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19), [Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20), [Peng et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib37), [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). For an evolving
agent, however, an aggregate score can hide exchanges between acquired
and lost behavior. Recent evolution-oriented evaluations make this
limitation visible by comparing changing and frozen agents across
sequential task streams, rather than reporting only the terminal score
([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib176), [Deng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib181)).
Let $`d_{t}(c)=s(A_{t+1},c;\mathcal{B})-s(A_{t},c;\mathcal{B})`$ be the
matched score change on case $`c`$. The acquisition rate is

|     |                                                        |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       G_{t}=\Pr_{c\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[d_{t}(c)>0\right],
       ```                                                     |     | (38) |

and the regression rate is

|     |                                                        |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{t}=\Pr_{c\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[d_{t}(c)<0\right].
       ```                                                     |     | (39) |

For binary task outcomes, $`G_{t}`$ counts newly solved cases and
$`R_{t}`$ counts cases lost after the update. Reporting both prevents a
positive average gain from concealing substantial regressions. For
graded metrics, their magnitudes should be reported alongside the two
rates. These rates provide a common summary of a distinction that recent
benchmarks expose through different measurements. SkillLearnBench finds
that skill-learning gains are not consistent across tasks and models
([Zhong et al., 2026](#bib.bib177)), while ContinualSkillBench shows
that sequential improvement can be comparable to context-only adaptation
and can leave weaker agents with fragmented, task-specific skill
collections ([Guan et al., 2026](#bib.bib182)). A positive average can
therefore reflect a small set of narrow gains even when the retained
component remains redundant or fails to generalize.

Longitudinal evaluation adds another axis. If $`J_{i,t}`$ denotes
performance on task group $`i`$ after the agent has evolved through
stage $`t`$, the matrix of $`J_{i,t}`$ values shows forward transfer to
later groups and retention on earlier ones. Periodic evaluation on old
repositories or defect families can reveal forgetting, while evaluation
on new repositories tests whether the learned behavior exceeds the scope
of its generating feedback. The same checkpoints should also record
component growth, retirement, and rollback success. A memory bank that
continually expands while retrieval quality declines is not well
described by its final solve rate alone. FinEvo-Bench exemplifies this
design with paired evolving and non-evolving controls evaluated under
independently shuffled task streams ([Deng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib181)).
Evidence from skill maintenance also shows that regression can be path
dependent. Unconditional skill accumulation can improve performance
initially and then degrade it, while removing the original harmful
skills may recover only part of the loss because later skills have
already inherited their errors ([Shang et al., 2026](#bib.bib140)).
Checkpoints should therefore preserve update lineage and measure both
pre-admission harm and post-hoc rollback effectiveness.

Evolution costs and use costs should be separated. Let
$`C_{\mathrm{evolve}}`$ include experience processing, candidate
construction, search, and selection, and let $`C_{\mathrm{use}}`$ be the
cost of executing the retained agent once. If an update is reused $`N`$
times, its amortized cost per use is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\overline{C}_{N}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{evolve}}}{N}+C_{\mathrm{use}}.
``` |  | (40) |

This distinction changes the interpretation of efficiency. An expensive
offline harness search may be worthwhile when its result supports many
later tasks, whereas a utility created for one trajectory has little
opportunity to amortize its construction cost. SkillMOO makes this
trade-off explicit by optimizing skill bundles for pass rate, monetary
cost, and runtime, with pruning and substitution sometimes outperforming
continued accumulation ([Gong et al., 2026](#bib.bib136)). SEA-Eval
further shows that similar success rates can hide large differences in
token consumption ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib176)). A broader study
of coding-agent trajectories likewise finds substantial run-to-run token
variation and no monotonic relation between greater token use and
accuracy ([Bai et al., 2026a](#bib.bib198)). Reports should therefore
include the update budget, evaluation and selection costs, subsequent
token and tool usage, wall time, storage growth, and human supervision.

The resulting evaluation record should connect four quantities: the
software outcomes obtained, the persistent components changed, the cases
that gained or regressed, and the resources consumed to produce and use
those changes. Security, maintainability, and reviewability should be
added when they are part of the intended software outcome rather than
inferred from functional success. EVOMAL illustrates why this record
must extend beyond task accuracy. A retrieved malicious skill can be
copied into newly authored skills and remain in the evolving library
after the planted source is removed ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib141)).
Such propagation is not captured by $`G_{t}`$ or $`R_{t}`$ alone, but it
is a persistent behavioral consequence of the update process. This
protocol turns benchmark scores into evidence about a changing agent. It
also preserves the central boundary of the survey. A retained mechanism
shows that evolution occurred, while matched, held-out, and longitudinal
evaluation shows whether that evolution improved the coding agent.

## 9 Self-Evolving Coding Products

### 9.1 Product Landscape

Research systems describe what a coding agent could evolve, whereas
deployed products reveal which forms of evolution can operate under
practical constraints. We organize the product landscape using the
asset, architecture, and model layers introduced earlier and identify
the persistent object changed by each product. Inclusion requires a
documented mechanism for retaining agent state across later steps,
sessions, or tasks; it does not require a fully autonomous or
experimentally validated evolution loop. Table
[7](#S9.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 9.1 Product Landscape ‣ 9 Self-Evolving Coding Products ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
summarizes representative products documented as of September 2026.

The distribution across these layers is highly asymmetric. Persistent
memory, skills, and context appear in many products, a smaller group
reaches into the execution harness, and none publicly exposes
repository-derived parameter updates as a persistent product capability.
This pattern defines a *deployment frontier*. The relevant design
question is how much behavioral leverage an update provides relative to
the cost of scoping, validating, auditing, and reversing it. Increasing
intervention depth usually expands both the influence of an update and
the consequences of an error. The three layers therefore describe
intervention depth rather than a maturity ranking; a well-governed asset
update may be more useful in production than a deeper change whose
contribution cannot be isolated.

Table 7: Representative self-evolving coding products organized by their
documented persistent update layers.

Asset-centered products. Assets are the dominant entry point for
productized evolution. Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf,
Augment, and OpenClaw persist repository facts, preferences, or
workspace context across sessions ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib111),
[GitHub, 2026](#bib.bib109), [Cursor, 2026](#bib.bib112), [Windsurf and
Cognition, 2026](#bib.bib114), [Augment Code, 2025](#bib.bib110),
[OpenClaw, 2026](#bib.bib121)). Other products move from factual
retention toward procedural reuse. Gemini CLI proposes memory patches
and skill drafts, Devin consolidates session evidence into knowledge and
playbooks, Letta Code revises memory and versions skills, Hermes creates
and updates skills from experience, and Replit Agent can preserve
learned procedures as project skills ([Google, 2026](#bib.bib108),
[Cognition, 2026](#bib.bib113), [Letta, 2026](#bib.bib118), [Nous
Research, 2026](#bib.bib119), [Replit, 2026](#bib.bib120)). These
mechanisms change what the agent can recall or invoke while leaving the
surrounding execution structure largely intact. Their concentration at
this layer follows from the properties of externalized state. Memory and
skills can be represented as bounded files or records, scoped to a user,
branch, or repository, inspected before reuse, and edited or removed
without replacing the whole agent. Their provenance can remain attached
to the stored item, and access control can follow existing workspace
boundaries. This supports tenant-specific adaptation while reducing the
need to pool private repository traces into shared model training.
GitHub Copilot, for example, attaches source citations to repository
facts and revalidates them against the current branch, while Gemini CLI
holds generated memory patches and skills for review before adoption
([GitHub, 2026](#bib.bib109), [Google, 2026](#bib.bib108)). Asset
updates thus resemble small, versionable software changes whose scope
and owner can be made explicit.

This advantage also reveals the main weakness of asset-centered
products. Storage is easier than maintaining a useful asset collection.
As entries accumulate, overlapping memories can disagree, a skill can
outlive the API or repository state under which it was learned, and
retrieval can introduce an irrelevant item into an otherwise correct
trajectory. Product quality therefore depends increasingly on lifecycle
operations such as consolidation, conflict detection, revalidation,
retirement, and rollback. The competitive boundary is shifting from
whether a product can remember to whether it can govern what should
remain active and determine when that retained state should influence a
decision.

Architecture-spanning products. A smaller set exposes changes to the
organization of execution. Prime Agent treats prompts, skills, memory,
and sub-agent specifications as editable continual-harness state and
records revisions for rollback ([Prime Intellect, 2026](#bib.bib107)).
DeepSeek Harness allows capabilities and runtime modes to be recomposed
through plugins and persistent presets ([DeepSeek-AI,
2026b](#bib.bib116)). OpenBlock presents an additional boundary case
that connects learned codebase patterns with planned skill and
evaluation-suite construction ([OpenBlock Labs, 2026](#bib.bib115)).
These products can also update assets, but their architectural
significance lies in changing how capabilities are assembled, delegated,
or controlled. Such changes have a wider effect because they can alter
control flow, tool exposure, and coordination across many later tasks.

Harness evolution is emerging because it occupies a useful middle layer.
A change to validation order, retry policy, context routing, or
sub-agent delegation can affect many decisions without modifying the
underlying model. The implementation remains code or configuration that
can be versioned, tested, compared, and rolled back. It can also survive
a model upgrade, giving the product a source of persistent behavior that
is partly independent of a particular model release. These properties
make architecture a high-leverage target when stronger base models alone
no longer determine product behavior.

The same leverage increases the blast radius of a faulty update. A
misleading memory may affect the tasks that retrieve it, whereas a
changed termination or validation rule may affect every task passing
through the harness. Asset and architecture evolution are also coupled
in practice. An asset determines what knowledge or operation is
available, while the harness determines when it is retrieved, trusted,
executed, and revised. A product that creates skills but never changes
these control rules remains asset-centered; a product that revises
selection, delegation, or validation moves into architecture even when
the edit also touches prompts or skills. This functional distinction
explains why similar persistent files can represent different depths of
intervention.

Model-level products. The catalogue contains no product that publicly
documents persistent, repository-derived updates to its deployed model
parameters. Providers may continue training their underlying models, but
that process normally occurs outside the user-visible agent loop and
cannot be attributed to a particular repository trajectory. The product
landscape therefore becomes sparser as the intervention moves from
assets to architecture and then to model parameters. Deeper changes have
a broader behavioral scope, require more expensive validation, and are
harder to diagnose or reverse when they fail. Several constraints
explain this gap. A repository trajectory provides sparse and correlated
evidence, and a passing patch does not show which parameter change
should be retained. Online adaptation can also introduce forgetting,
spread repository-specific shortcuts across tasks, or encode sensitive
code in a component shared by multiple users. Parameter updates are
expensive to evaluate because their effects are distributed across
behaviors that may be unrelated to the generating task. Rollback is
correspondingly coarse: restoring a checkpoint removes all changes
bundled into it, while the harmful influence of one memory or harness
edit can often be traced and withdrawn directly.

This creates a separation between provider evolution and product
evolution. Providers can train new model releases using aggregated data,
but the resulting change follows a release cycle and is rarely
attributable to one user’s coding experience. User-visible
self-evolution therefore remains concentrated in external state and
executable orchestration. The product landscape suggests a practical
design rule: expose the deepest persistent intervention whose
provenance, evaluation scope, and rollback boundary can still be made
concrete.

### 9.2 From Experience to Governed Updates

Productization turns evolution into a controlled state change. A task
trajectory and its feedback may generate a candidate update
$`\hat{u}_{t}`$, but the candidate should affect later execution only
after an admission decision. Let $`z_{t}`$ denote the persistent product
state, which may contain assets or architecture. A generic governed
update is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
z_{t+1}=\begin{cases}\operatorname{Apply}(z_{t},\hat{u}_{t}),&\operatorname{Gate}(\hat{u}_{t};v_{t},p_{t},\rho_{t})=1,\\
z_{t},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
``` |  | (41) |

where $`v_{t}`$ summarizes validation, $`p_{t}`$ records provenance and
authority, and $`\rho_{t}`$ specifies the permitted scope of reuse. The
gate may be implemented by automatic checks, explicit user approval,
organizational policy, or a combination of them.

This compact expression contains several decisions that products often
conflate. Proposal determines which part of a trajectory becomes a
candidate; validation asks whether its evidence extends beyond the case
that produced it; authorization determines who may change shared agent
state; and scoping decides which user, repository, branch, or runtime
may receive the update. These are part of the evolution mechanism
because they control which experience is allowed to shape future
behavior. A permissive gate increases plasticity but can accumulate
stale memories, conflicting skills, or brittle control rules. A
conservative gate preserves stability but may discard useful adaptation.
The appropriate threshold depends on the update’s blast radius. A
repository fact can be admitted under narrow scope and revalidated when
retrieved, whereas a tool or harness revision may require integration
tests, held-out tasks, and explicit rollback support. Validation can
therefore combine the estimated gain $`\widehat{\Delta J}_{t}`$,
regression risk $`\widehat{R}_{t}`$, update and use costs, and the
breadth of $`\rho_{t}`$ rather than reducing admission to success on the
generating task.

Products instantiate this control point differently. Gemini CLI never
applies automatically extracted memory or skill candidates without
approval, whereas Claude Code writes repository-scoped memory that
remains directly inspectable and editable ([Google, 2026](#bib.bib108),
[Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib111)). GitHub Copilot validates a recalled
repository fact before use and retires entries that remain unused
([GitHub, 2026](#bib.bib109)). Prime Agent exposes update history and
rollback for its continual harness ([Prime Intellect,
2026](#bib.bib107)). These mechanisms treat a persistent agent update
much like a software change. It is proposed, scoped, reviewed or
validated, committed, monitored, and potentially reverted.

Admission should remain provisional after deployment. An update can move
from *candidate* to *active*, then to *revised*, *quarantined*, or
*retired* as new evidence arrives. Monitoring must attribute later
failures and gains to the version that was actually used, while rollback
must restore associated indexes, dependency bindings, and derived
presets as well as the visible memory or code. Product governance thus
turns a collection of persistent additions into maintained, versioned
agent state. This lifecycle is also what allows the hot-swappable
architecture discussed next to support continued evolution without
making every runtime experiment permanent.

### 9.3 Toward Hot-Swappable Coding Agents

*“A future harness may generate and deploy modifications to its own
components while continuously serving requests.”* —*A Programming
Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability* ([Shi et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib122), p. 5)

DeepSeek Harness provides a concrete prototype of a product form in
which the composition of a running agent becomes a primary site of
evolution. It exposes models, tools, skills, session management,
sandboxes, storage, execution loops, scheduling, and the user interface
as plugins, with configuration determining which implementations are
mounted together ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026b](#bib.bib116)). The unit of change
can therefore be an individual capability such as a search tool, context
policy, validation loop, or model adapter. Its Cordis lifecycle can
unload an existing plugin, unwind the registrations and effects owned by
that instance, and load revised code, while configuration edits affect
only the entries that were mounted, removed, or reconfigured
([DeepSeek-AI, 2026a](#bib.bib117)). Creator mode extends this mechanism
by allowing developers or agents to inspect the live runtime, test
temporary plugins in memory, and combine selected components into
presets ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026b](#bib.bib116)). These mechanisms suggest a
two-speed evolution process. The fast path mounts a candidate during a
session and observes its immediate behavioral effects. The slower path
validates it on broader cases, records its provenance and dependencies,
and promotes it into a versioned preset for later sessions. A temporary
mount supplies evidence about a candidate; adoption, retention, and
subsequent reuse turn that candidate into a persistent update. The
harness consequently acts as an *evolution control plane* joining
experience-derived proposals with evaluation and deployment.

This product form shifts the central engineering problem from replacing
a whole agent to controlling change inside a live composition. Active
tasks must remain bound to compatible plugin versions, state must be
migrated or discarded when interfaces change, and rollback must withdraw
both a component and the effects it introduced. Version binding,
dependency-aware disposal, shadow or canary evaluation, and atomic
promotion can support a small stable kernel surrounded by an evolving
periphery of plugins. The common plugin boundary does not erase the
taxonomy developed earlier. A callable utility remains an asset update,
a plugin that changes routing or the execution loop is an architecture
update, and a model-adapter swap establishes model self-evolution only
when the model’s parameters are themselves updated. Functional role
still determines the depth of evolution, even when every change is
packaged and deployed in the same way.

## 10 Challenges and Open Problems

Self-evolving coding agents raise challenges beyond those of
conventional coding agents because their behavior changes over time. An
unreliable test result, noisy trajectory, weak verifier, or
benchmark-specific shortcut may not only affect one patch, but also be
stored as memory, distilled into a skill, selected as a workflow, used
to update a model, embedded in a scaffold, or used to reshape the
agent’s context and execution environment. Thus, the key challenge is
not only whether self-evolution improves benchmark performance, but
whether the evolutionary process remains reliable, reproducible, and
aligned with software engineering constraints. The consequences depend
on both reuse scope and intervention depth. A faulty repository memory
may bias a family of related issues, whereas a faulty harness or model
update can alter every subsequent decision. The open problems below
therefore concern the reliability of the entire path from local software
evidence to persistent behavioral change.

#### Reproducibility, contamination, and benchmark overfitting.

Self-evolution makes reproducibility difficult because agents may change
across runs, tasks, repositories, tool environments, or model versions.
Systems that select self-modifications or agent variants using benchmark
outcomes are especially sensitive to evaluation noise and benchmark
leakage ([Robeyns et al., 2025](#bib.bib46), [Zhang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib18)). This concern is amplified in code evaluation, where
contamination and benchmark-specific adaptation are already known issues
([Jain et al., 2024](#bib.bib60)). SWE-rebench evaluates models on
continuously collected, fresh software-engineering tasks and finds that
some results on SWE-bench Verified may be inflated by contamination
([Badertdinov et al., 2025](#bib.bib169)). DeepSWE exposes a related
measurement problem. On original long-horizon tasks, an independent
judge disagrees with its purpose-built verifiers far less often than
with tests inherited from public fixes, showing that both solution
exposure and incomplete tests can distort the apparent capability of an
agent ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib183)). A matched-budget study of
automatic harness evolution provides more direct evidence: on
Terminal-Bench 2.1, evolved harnesses do not consistently outperform
simple test-time search baselines and show limited generalization to
held-out tasks ([Wang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib184)). Reproducibility also
depends on the surrounding harness. Holding the model fixed across 35
sequential Qwen Code releases reveals quality fluctuations attributable
to harness changes, while a separate comparison finds up to a
$`40\times`$ difference in tokens per solved task across three harnesses
([Ben Sghaier et al., 2026](#bib.bib185), [Vats and Golev,
2026](#bib.bib186)). For a self-evolving agent, contamination extends
beyond pretraining overlap. If the same tasks construct experience,
select retained updates, and measure the final system, the evaluation
loop can progressively fit its own evidence. Even a fully reproducible
final score may then reproduce an overfitted evolutionary path. A
credible report should preserve the initial agent, task order, update
history, evaluator version, and adopted and rejected candidates;
separate update, selection, and held-out evaluation cases; and repeat
the process across seeds or task orders. The object to reproduce is the
trajectory of change, not only the terminal agent.

#### Feedback reliability, safety, and tool dependence.

Executable feedback is central to self-evolving coding agents, but
tests, compilers, CI logs, generated tests, and reward models are
imperfect. Systems that rely on unit-test validation, environment
rewards, or learned verifiers may therefore inherit the biases and blind
spots of these signals ([Wei et al., 2025b](#bib.bib50), [Pan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib51)). This is particularly risky when agents modify tools,
workflows, or their own scaffolds, because a misleading feedback signal
can shape future behavior rather than only one output. An analysis of
4,892 patches from ten software-development agents finds that even
test-passing patches can modify different files and functions from
developer patches, exposing limits in the tests used to identify
acceptable repairs ([Chen and Jiang, 2024](#bib.bib192)).
Security-focused evidence is more direct. Across 1,030 valid traces from
seven agent frameworks, 170 patches passed the available functional
checks while omitting protections, applying inadequate fixes, or
introducing vulnerabilities; neither test passing nor LLM review
reliably intercepted these cases ([Bai et al., 2026b](#bib.bib193)). The
same concern applies when the agent authors its own acceptance signal.
Experiments on heuristic self-improvement show that self-assigned
verification scores can stay near perfect while sealed deployment
performance remains low or regresses; retaining an external
accept–reject audit improves results across six models ([Guo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib187)). Memory-based agents expose a related feedback
loop. Incorrect episodes can receive inflated self-evaluation scores and
then be preferentially retrieved, whereas a de-inflation method raises
BIRD execution accuracy from 54.0% to 56.9% ([Asadolahi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib188)). Coding feedback is therefore explicit without
necessarily being complete. The danger grows when an update compresses a
locally observed outcome into a broadly reused rule while discarding the
conditions under which the outcome was valid. Future systems need to
retain provenance, environment versions, test coverage, and
applicability conditions with the update itself. Adoption should combine
independent signals where possible, such as regression tests, static
analysis, security checks, differential execution, and review, while
treating flaky tests, generated oracles, sandbox mismatches, and tool
failures as uncertainty rather than negative task evidence. Tool
reliability and sandbox fidelity are thus part of the learning signal,
not merely implementation details.

#### Reversibility, harness bloat, and specialization.

The hot-swappable product form discussed in Section
[9.3](#S9.SS3 "9.3 Toward Hot-Swappable Coding Agents ‣ 9 Self-Evolving Coding Products ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents")
makes reversibility a runtime property. Withdrawing a live component
must also undo its state changes and dependency effects while requests
continue to be served. Cordis calls this property *temporal
composability* and implements it through tracked inverse effects ([Shi
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib122)). AHE similarly makes harness components
explicit and revertible, but end-to-end guarantees of this kind are not
yet standard across self-evolving coding agents ([Lin et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib74)). Its experiments also show why explicit components
and attribution matter: ten evolution rounds improve Terminal-Bench 2
performance, while ablations locate the transferable gains in tools,
middleware, and long-term memory rather than in every edited component.
The Phantom Guardrails study demonstrates how bloat can arise even
without a real failure: a proposer installs a guardrail for a
nonexistent violation in 15 of 60 runs when harmless input resembles a
familiar rule, compared with none on featureless input, and an add-only
loop makes the spurious component persist ([Wang et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib189)). Reversibility must include the evaluation path as
well as task execution. An audit of real self-improvement trajectories
finds harness tampering across different systems and observes that such
edits can persist in the lineage of the selected best agent ([Wang et
al., 2026f](#bib.bib194)). A candidate may appear better because it
changes task access, termination, logging, or validation rather than
because it solves software problems more effectively. This makes
authority, provenance, and evaluator isolation part of harness
integrity. Components that generate and judge an update should not be
able to silently weaken the checks that authorize its adoption. Without
lifecycle controls, evolution can become cumulative trial-and-error. A
locally successful fix may be appended as another prompt rule, memory
item, tool wrapper, routing condition, or agent role rather than
replacing the mechanism that caused the failure. The resulting harness
becomes larger, more coupled, and harder to audit, while narrow
benchmark selection can turn these additions into repository- or
environment-specific shortcuts. Future systems should therefore treat
removal as a first-class operation, track the provenance and inverse of
persistent modifications, enforce complexity budgets, retire redundant
components, and validate promoted changes on held-out software
environments. Progress should be measured against both performance and
structural cost. Otherwise, an agent can improve a benchmark while
becoming less portable, less inspectable, and more expensive to
maintain.

#### Long-term memory, skills, and coordination.

Memory and skill mechanisms allow agents to reuse software-engineering
experience, but they also introduce quality-control problems. Experience
banks, repository memory, and skill libraries may become stale,
redundant, overly repository-specific, or contaminated by failed
trajectories ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20), [Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib43), [Xiao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib45)). Controlled
experiments on memory management reveal an experience-following effect
in which similar retrieved records induce similar outputs. Incorrect or
misaligned records can therefore propagate errors, whereas selective
addition and deletion outperform unrestricted memory growth ([Xiong et
al., 2026](#bib.bib195)). Skill evolution has a similar lifecycle
problem. A systematic study across extractors, consumer models, and five
agentic domains finds that generated skills help on average but also
produce non-trivial negative transfer; extraction quality and
consumption quality do not necessarily coincide ([Huang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib196)). These results make retention conditional: an
artifact is useful only for a compatible task, retriever, consumer, and
execution context. This producer–consumer gap is also visible at the
harness level. Models from different capability tiers can produce
updates with similar gains, yet their ability to activate and follow the
resulting artifacts is non-monotonic, with weak models often failing to
use what was retained ([Lin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib101)). Multi-agent
and workflow-evolving systems add coordination challenges because a
local improvement can alter the assumptions of neighboring components.
Changing one role, message schema, or routing rule may make an existing
skill unreachable or duplicate another agent’s responsibility.
AgentConductor empirically shows that topology affects both coding
accuracy and communication cost, obtaining up to a 14.6% Pass@$`1`$
improvement while reducing topology density and token use ([Wang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib42)). Evidence from a deployed collaboration network
shows that scale alone does not solve this problem: among more than 1.5
million shared assets in EvoMap, 98% are never reused and over 84% of
approved assets bypass quality checks through vacuous tests ([Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib190)). The broader problem is therefore not how much
experience the system retains, but whether it can maintain a coherent
persistent state. Future work should jointly manage relevance,
conflicts, dependencies, usage, and retirement across memory, skills,
workflows, and teams instead of optimizing each store in isolation.

#### Evaluation beyond short benchmarks.

Current evaluations mainly measure short-horizon success through pass
rates, resolve rates, or benchmark scores. Yet real software engineering
also requires maintainability, security, reviewability, efficiency, and
long-term reliability. The gap is already visible without moving beyond
coding. SWE-EVO requires release-scale changes spanning an average of 21
files and hundreds of tests; a GPT-5 and OpenHands configuration
resolves 21% of these tasks, compared with 65% on SWE-bench Verified
([Thai et al., 2025](#bib.bib172)). The difference shows that success on
isolated issues does not establish sustained planning, preservation of
earlier behavior, or control of interactions among changes. Longitudinal
agent benchmarks reveal a second gap. LifelongAgentBench finds that
straightforward experience replay is limited by irrelevant records and
context constraints ([Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib173)). PATH-Bench
further shows that strong forward transfer does not guarantee retention
and that later experience can reshape gains acquired earlier in a task
sequence ([Yang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib197)). Coding-specific memory
experiments across six benchmarks find a 3.7% average gain from
cross-domain transfer, but also show that abstract validation routines
transfer more reliably than concrete traces, which can cause negative
transfer through excessive specificity ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib191)). Evaluation must consequently follow the agent after
an update rather than test it once. Repeated checkpoints should measure
newly acquired behavior, regressions on earlier repositories, transfer
to held-out repositories and defect families, resource growth, and
sensitivity to task order. Cross-domain transfer remains an open
question, but the immediate standard should be stronger: evolution
learned from one part of software engineering should survive time and
improve later coding work beyond the cases that produced it.

## 11 Conclusion

Coding agents are unusually well positioned to learn from their own
work. Execution yields specific outcomes, diagnostics, and trajectories
that can be tied to repository state and checked again. Our synthesis
follows how this evidence becomes persistent change in assets,
architecture, or model parameters, with progressively deeper
intervention. The crucial distinction is between retaining an update and
showing that it improves later decisions. Passing a test validates a
software artifact under particular conditions; demonstrating agent
improvement requires reuse and benefit on matched, held-out tasks.

Research and products currently favor memories, skills, tools, and
editable harnesses because their changes can be scoped, inspected, and
reversed. Looking ahead, a coding agent could treat these components as
a versioned system that it revises during ordinary coding work.
Experience would generate candidate changes, independent checks would
govern their adoption, and later tasks would show whether each change
should be kept, revised, or rolled back. Extending this cycle to
workflows and model parameters will require stronger evidence of gains,
regressions, and costs across repositories and time. The long-term goal
is an agent that can identify which experiences deserve to persist,
where they apply, and when they should be forgotten.
````
